items.q: An adult patient with chronic tibial osteomyelitis is evaluated. Radiographs and CT show a full-thickness cortical sequestrum that can be excised surgically without compromising the mechanical stability of the bone. According to the Cierny-Mader classification system, what is the anatomical type of this infection?
items.e: Cierny-Mader Type III (Localised) osteomyelitis is characterized by full-thickness cortical sequestration that can be excised without loss of structural stability. Type I is intramedullary, Type II involves the superficial cortex secondary to soft-tissue defects, and Type IV is a diffuse, mechanically unstable lesion.
items.note: Accurate, clear single-best-answer testing Cierny-Mader anatomical staging.

items.q: According to the international consensus definition for Fracture-Related Infection (FRI), which of the following is classified as a suggestive criterion rather than a confirmatory criterion?
o: Fistula or sinus tract communicating with the bone or implant
Presence of purulent drainage encountered during surgical exploration
Persistent new wound drainage beyond the first few post-operative days
Histopathology showing more than 5 neutrophils per high-power field
items.e: Persistent or new wound drainage beyond the first few post-operative days is a suggestive criterion for FRI that warrants further work-up. Confirmatory criteria include a communicating sinus/fistula, intraoperative pus, phenotypically identical pathogens in two deep samples, or >5 neutrophils/HPF on histopathology.
items.note: Directly tests consensus criteria for FRI with clear separation of suggestive vs confirmatory parameters.

items.q: A 22-year-old man presents with dull metaphyseal pain in the distal femur. Plain radiographs reveal a lucent lesion with a sclerotic border. MRI shows a rim of slightly hyperintense T1 signal lining the cavity (the "penumbra sign"). What histological component gives rise to this characteristic MRI finding in a Brodie abscess?
o: Vascularised granulation tissue lining the abscess wall
items.e: The "penumbra sign" on T1-weighted MRI is a rim of slightly higher signal intensity lining an abscess cavity, representing vascularised granulation tissue. It is characteristic of subacute osteomyelitis (Brodie abscess) and helps differentiate it from skeletal neoplasms.
items.note: High-yield MRI sign question testing exact pathological correlate.

items.q: During arthroscopic evaluation of a septic knee joint, the surgeon notes aggressive pannus formation that is actively infiltrating and undermining joint cartilage, accompanied by subchondral osteolysis on radiographs. According to the Gachter staging system, what is the stage and appropriate surgical management?
o: Stage II; Arthroscopic lavage and fibrin debridement
Stage IV; Open arthrotomy, synovectomy, and debridement
Stage I; Repeated closed needle aspirations
items.e: Gachter Stage IV septic arthritis is defined by aggressive pannus infiltrating and undermining cartilage with radiological subchondral osteolysis. At this stage, open arthrotomy, radical synovectomy, and debridement are required, whereas Stages I to III can be treated arthroscopically.
items.note: Standard Gachter classification question with clear treatment implications.

items.q: A patient undergoes staged reconstruction of a 6 cm segmental tibial defect secondary to debrided chronic osteomyelitis using the Masquelet induced-membrane technique. Following the first stage (radical debridement, stabilization, and placement of a PMMA spacer), at what interval should the second stage (spacer removal and autologous cancellous bone grafting) typically be performed?
items.e: In the Masquelet technique, the PMMA spacer induces a biological membrane rich in growth factors (VEGF, TGF-beta, BMP-2). The second stage—removing the spacer while preserving the membrane and packing the cavity with cancellous autograft—is performed at 4 to 8 weeks.
items.note: Standard timing question for Masquelet technique.

items.q: A 23-year-old sexually active female presents with fever, migratory polyarthralgias, painless pustular skin lesions over her extremities, and acute wrist tenosynovitis. What is the recommended first-line definitive antibiotic therapy for this presentation?
o: Intravenous Ceftriaxone 1 g daily for approximately 7 days
items.e: The clinical triad of tenosynovitis, painless pustular dermatitis, and migratory polyarthralgia is classic for disseminated gonococcal infection (Neisseria gonorrhoeae). Standard treatment is IV ceftriaxone 1 g daily (switched to oral after improvement) for a total duration of about 7 days.
items.note: Classic presentation and guideline regimen for disseminated gonococcal infection.

items.q: A 60-year-old male with a 35-year history of chronic osteomyelitis of the tibia presents with an enlarging, foul-smelling mass with everted edges at the cutaneous orifice of a long-standing sinus tract. What is the most likely diagnosis to be confirmed on tissue biopsy?
items.e: Malignant transformation of a long-standing chronic osteomyelitis sinus tract is termed a Marjolin ulcer, which is almost exclusively a squamous cell carcinoma occurring after a latency period of decades. Clinical features include foul or bloody discharge, everted edges, and a fungating mass.
items.note: Standard high-yield question regarding chronic osteomyelitis complications.

items.q: A 45-year-old marine aquarium enthusiast develops chronic indolent granulomatous tenosynovitis of the flexor tendon sheath in his index finger after cleaning a fish tank. Tissue biopsy specimens should be cultured at which temperature range to isolate the suspected pathogen?
items.e: Mycobacterium marinum causes granulomatous tenosynovitis following marine or fish tank exposure. Because M. marinum grows preferentially at lower temperatures than typical pathogens, microbiology specimens must be cultured at 30°C - 32°C.
items.note: Specific microbiology culture requirement question frequently tested in superspeciality exams.

items.q: A 14-year-old boy presents with right hip pain of 3 months' duration. Physical examination shows the limb held in flexion, abduction, and external rotation, with apparent lengthening. Plain radiographs demonstrate juxta-articular osteopenia with preservation of the joint space. According to the Tuli clinical and radiological staging of hip tuberculosis, what is the stage and the expected outcome with non-operative treatment?
o: Stage I (Synovitis); near-normal function expected with ATT, traction, and mobilization
Stage II (Early arthritis); high likelihood of fibrous ankylosis despite ATT
Stage I (Synovitis); immediate synovectomy and joint debridement required
Stage II (Early arthritis); apparent lengthening necessitates immediate Girdlestone excision
items.e: Stage I (Synovitis) in hip tuberculosis is characterized by flexion, abduction, and external rotation with apparent lengthening, accompanied by osteopenia and preserved joint space. Conservative management with ATT, traction, and gradual mobilization yields near-normal functional recovery.
items.note: Accurate clinical staging question according to Tuli's classification of hip TB.

items.q: A 35-year-old man on antitubercular therapy for tuberculous arthritis of the knee complains of difficulty distinguishing between red and green traffic lights and notices decreased visual acuity. Which drug in his regimen is responsible for this side effect, and what is its mechanism/type of action?
o: Isoniazid; bactericidal drug causing peripheral neuritis
Ethambutol; bacteriostatic drug causing optic neuritis
Pyrazinamide; sterilizing drug causing hyperuricemic neuropathy
Rifampicin; sterilizing drug causing cranial nerve toxicity
items.e: Ethambutol is a bacteriostatic antitubercular agent that can cause retrobulbar optic neuritis, which clinically manifests as reduced visual acuity and loss of red-green color vision.
items.note: Standard high-yield pharmacology facts tested accurately.

items.q: A 42-year-old male presents with a painless, slowly enlarging mass over the volar aspect of his right wrist and distal forearm. On examination, pressing the proximal swelling causes fluid and fullness to bulge distal to the flexor retinaculum (cross-fluctuation). Operative exploration reveals multiple small, smooth, oval 'melon-seed' bodies within the flexor sheaths. What is this clinical entity?
items.e: Compound palmar ganglion is tuberculous tenosynovitis of the flexor sheaths of the wrist and hand. It presents with cross-fluctuation above and below the flexor retinaculum and contains melon-seed (rice) bodies.
items.note: Classic presentation and pathology of tuberculous tenosynovitis in the hand/wrist.

items.q: A 4-year-old child is brought with painless, fusiform swellings of the proximal phalanges and metacarpals of the hand. Radiographs show ballooned, expanded short tubular bones with marked cortical thinning ('spina ventosa') without sequestra. Which statement regarding tuberculous dactylitis is correct?
o: It affects long bones of the leg more commonly than short tubular bones of the hand
Syphilitic dactylitis is characteristically bilateral and symmetrical, helping differentiate it from spina ventosa
Massive sequestra formation and dense sclerosis are classic early radiological findings
Surgical curettage and bone grafting are mandatory first-line treatments in all pediatric cases
items.e: Tuberculous dactylitis (spina ventosa) affects the short tubular bones of the hand more than the foot in young children. Syphilitic dactylitis is a key differential diagnosis that is typically bilateral and symmetrical.
items.note: Accurate details regarding spina ventosa and its main differential diagnosis.

items.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with chronic monoarticular pain and boggy swelling of the knee joint. Radiographs reveal the classic Phemister triad of tuberculous arthritis. Which of the following features constitute this triad?
o: Juxta-articular osteoporosis, peripheral (marginal) erosions, and gradual narrowing of the joint space
Rapid joint space loss, subchondral sclerosis, and exuberant osteophytes
Central punched-out erosions, periosteal apposition, and dense bone sequestra
Soft tissue calcification, pathological dislocation, and intercondylar notch widening
items.e: The Phemister triad of tuberculous arthritis consists of: 1) Juxta-articular osteoporosis (osteopenia), 2) Peripheral (marginal) bone erosions, and 3) Gradual narrowing of the joint space due to slow cartilage destruction.
items.note: Classic triad cleanly tested with standard orthopaedic distractors.

items.q: An outbreak of chronic, non-healing surgical site infections with persistent sinuses is observed in an orthopaedic unit following elective arthroscopic procedures. Cultures isolate rapidly growing non-tuberculous mycobacteria that are resistant to standard first-line ATT. Which organisms are most commonly responsible for such post-surgical outbreaks?
o: Mycobacterium fortuitum, M. chelonae, and M. abscessus
items.e: Rapidly growing mycobacteria, specifically Mycobacterium fortuitum, M. chelonae, and M. abscessus, are recognized causes of post-surgical and post-injection outbreaks in India, requiring specialized regimens (e.g., macrolides, amikacin) and debridement.
items.note: Well-established outbreak etiology in Indian orthopaedic practice.

items.q: A 30-year-old manual laborer with advanced, painful tuberculous destruction of the knee joint undergoes surgical arthrodesis to obtain a stable, pain-free limb. In which optimal position should the knee joint be fused?
o: 0-15 degrees flexion, 5-8 degrees valgus, and about 10 degrees external rotation
30-40 degrees flexion, 0 degrees valgus, and 15 degrees internal rotation
Full extension (0 degrees), 10 degrees varus, and neutral rotation
20-30 degrees flexion, 5 degrees varus, and 10 degrees internal rotation
items.e: The standard surgical alignment for knee arthrodesis is approximately 0-15 degrees of flexion, 5-8 degrees of valgus, and 10 degrees of external rotation.
items.note: Correct surgical fusion parameters for the knee.

items.q: A biopsy specimen from a patient with chronic hip tuberculosis undergoes diagnostic testing. Line probe assay (LPA) confirms resistance to both isoniazid and rifampicin, but susceptibility to fluoroquinolones, bedaquiline, and linezolid. How is this drug-resistance profile defined?
items.e: Multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) is defined as resistance to at least both isoniazid and rifampicin. Resistance to a fluoroquinolone in addition to MDR defines Pre-XDR TB.
items.note: Precise WHO/NTEP definition of drug-resistant tuberculosis.

items.q: A 2-year-old child presents with severe bowing of the lower limbs, short stature, and sparse scalp hair (alopecia). Laboratory testing reveals low serum calcium, low serum phosphate, elevated alkaline phosphatase, and elevated PTH. Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels are normal, but 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol) levels are extremely high. Which of the following is the underlying defect?
items.e: Vitamin D-dependent rickets type 2 (VDDR type 2) is caused by a vitamin D receptor defect. It presents with calcipenic rickets, alopecia, and characteristic markedly elevated serum 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol) levels.
items.note: Fully accurate, highly classic SS exam question on vitamin D pathway disorders.

items.q: Histologically, rickets is primarily a disorder affecting which specific zone of the growth plate (physis)?
items.e: In rickets, low phosphate prevents apoptosis of hypertrophic chondrocytes, causing the hypertrophic zone (zone of provisional calcification) to widen, splay, and fail to calcify properly.
items.note: Classic core histology concept tested in SS entrance exams.

items.q: A 6-year-old boy presents with hypophosphataemic rickets. Serum chemistry reveals low phosphate, normal calcium, and suppressed FGF23 levels. Serum 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is elevated, and 24-hour urine analysis demonstrates severe hypercalciuria. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.e: Hereditary hypophosphataemic rickets with hypercalciuria (HHRH) is caused by SLC34A3 mutations. It is distinguished from FGF23-mediated rickets (like XLH) by low FGF23, elevated calcitriol, and prominent hypercalciuria.
items.note: High-yield differentiation among phosphopenic rickets types.

items.q: Which surgical intervention is the initial procedure of choice for a 5-year-old child with persistent genu varum due to nutritional rickets who has achieved complete metabolic control but retains significant mechanical axis deviation and at least 2 years of growth remaining?
o: Acute opening-wedge proximal tibial osteotomy with plate fixation
Gradual multiplanar correction using an Ilizarov external fixator
Telescopic intramedullary rodding of the tibia and femur
items.e: Guided growth (temporary hemiepiphysiodesis using 8-plates) is the first surgical choice for coronal angular deformities around the knee in a growing child with remaining growth, provided metabolic control has already been established.
items.note: Standard paediatric orthopaedic surgical guideline statement.

items.q: Double tetracycline-labelled transiliac bone biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosing osteomalacia. Which of the following parameters on histomorphometry confirms osteomalacia?
o: Osteoid seam thickness under 5 µm with mineralisation lag time under 20 days
Osteoid seam thickness over 15 µm with mineralisation lag time over 100 days
Subperiosteal bone resorption with osteoclast tunneling
Widened zone of proliferation with empty chondrocyte lacunae
items.e: On double tetracycline-labelled bone biopsy, osteomalacia is pathognomonic for an increased osteoid seam thickness (>15 µm) and a prolonged mineralisation lag time exceeding 100 days.
items.note: Clear, objective quantitative criteria from pathology/orthopaedics notes.

items.q: All of the following are classic, typical anatomical locations for Looser zones (pseudofractures) in osteomalacia EXCEPT:
o: Medial aspect of the femoral neck
Convex (lateral) cortex of the subtrochanteric femoral shaft
items.e: Looser zones in osteomalacia occur typically on the concave/compression side of bones (such as the medial femoral neck, axillary border of the scapula, and pubic rami). Pseudofractures on the convex (lateral) cortex of the femoral shaft suggest atypical femoral fractures or Paget's disease.
items.note: Crucial distinction between Looser zones and atypical femoral fractures / Paget's disease.

items.q: According to the 2016 Global Consensus guidelines (Munns et al.), what is the single high-dose oral vitamin D (stoss therapy) option for treating nutritional rickets in a 4-year-old child?
items.e: According to the 2016 Global Consensus guidelines, the single high-dose stoss therapy option for nutritional rickets in children aged over 1 year to 12 years is 150,000 IU of vitamin D.
items.note: Direct reference to the standard Global Consensus guidelines dosing table.

items.q: Which of the following clinical features is typically ABSENT in children with X-linked hypophosphataemic rickets (XLH) compared to those with nutritional calcipenic rickets?
items.e: Proximal muscle weakness (myopathy), hypotonia, and hypocalcaemic tetany occur in calcipenic forms of rickets but are notably absent in XLH, where serum calcium levels remain normal.
items.note: High-yield clinical distinction between calcipenic and phosphopenic rickets.

items.q: Nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates (such as alendronate and zoledronate) exert their antiresorptive action on osteoclasts primarily by inhibiting which of the following enzymes?
items.e: Nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates inhibit farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase in the mevalonate pathway. This prevents prenylation of small GTPases required for osteoclast survival and ruffled border formation, leading to osteoclast apoptosis.
items.note: Accurate, well-framed question directly supported by reference notes.

items.q: A 68-year-old woman with severe postmenopausal osteoporosis was treated with subcutaneous denosumab 60 mg every 6 months for 4 years. She missed her next scheduled dose and stopped treatment entirely 8 months ago. She now presents with severe acute back pain, and radiographs reveal multiple new lumbar vertebral compression fractures. What is the primary pathophysiological mechanism responsible for this presentation?
o: Rebound surge in bone turnover and rapid bone loss following denosumab withdrawal
items.e: Discontinuing denosumab causes a rebound surge in osteoclast activity, rapid loss of bone mineral density, and an increased risk of multiple spontaneous vertebral fractures within 7 to 12 months. Denosumab should never be stopped without switching to a follow-on antiresorptive agent such as a bisphosphonate.
items.note: High-yield clinical scenario accurately testing denosumab withdrawal rebound effect.

items.q: A 72-year-old woman with severe osteoporosis (lumbar spine T-score -3.2) and a recent wrist fragility fracture is being evaluated for sequential treatment. Her past medical history is significant for an ischemic stroke 8 months ago. Which of the following osteoporosis medications is contraindicated in this patient?
items.e: In the ARCH trial, romosozumab demonstrated an increased risk of serious cardiovascular events (myocardial infarction and stroke) compared to alendronate. It is strictly contraindicated in patients with a myocardial infarction or stroke within the preceding 12 months.
items.note: Fully correct and standard guideline/trial-based contraindication question.

items.q: Which of the following clinical scenarios represents an absolute contraindication to initiating teriparatide therapy for osteoporosis?
o: Mild to moderate renal impairment (creatinine clearance 40 mL/min)
History of prior radiation therapy to the skeleton
Prior history of an osteoporotic hip fracture
items.e: Teriparatide is contraindicated in patients with prior skeletal radiation therapy, Paget disease of bone, unexplained elevated alkaline phosphatase, open epiphyses, hypercalcaemia, or skeletal malignancies, due to a theoretical increased risk of osteosarcoma or exacerbation of hypercalcaemia.
items.note: Standard board-style contraindication question, entirely accurate.

items.q: A 70-year-old woman taking oral alendronate for 7 years presents with subacute left mid-thigh pain. Radiographs demonstrate focal periosteal cortical thickening ('beaking') on the lateral mid-diaphysis of the left femur with an incomplete transverse fracture line. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Continue alendronate, prescribe full weight-bearing, and repeat radiographs in 6 months
Stop alendronate, obtain full-length radiographs of the right femur, restrict weight-bearing, and schedule prophylactic intramedullary nailing of the left femur
Stop alendronate and perform open reduction with plate and screw fixation of the left femur
Switch alendronate to denosumab 60 mg subcutaneously and encourage immediate range of motion exercises
items.e: An incomplete atypical femoral fracture (AFF) with prodromal thigh pain or a visible lateral cortex fracture line requires stopping the bisphosphonate, imaging the contralateral femur to exclude bilateral involvement, restricting weight-bearing, and performing prophylactic intramedullary nailing.
items.note: Excellent orthopaedic management question adhering strictly to ASBMR and clinical standards.

items.q: A 74-year-old man undergoes internal fixation of a low-trauma intertrochanteric hip fracture. He is vitamin D replete with normal renal function. According to the HORIZON-RFT trial, administering an annual intravenous zoledronic acid 5 mg infusion post-operatively yields which of the following proven clinical benefits?
o: Reduces both new clinical fractures and all-cause mortality
Reduces deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism rates
items.e: The HORIZON-RFT trial showed that giving intravenous zoledronate 5 mg annually after surgical repair of a low-trauma hip fracture reduced the rate of new clinical fractures by approximately 35% and reduced all-cause mortality by approximately 28%.
items.note: Classic landmark trial question, completely accurate.

items.q: A 62-year-old postmenopausal woman with osteopenia (lumbar spine T-score -2.2) and a strong family history of breast cancer is being considered for medical therapy. Which of the following correctly describes the efficacy profile of raloxifene established in landmark trials?
o: Reduces vertebral, hip, and non-vertebral fracture risk
Reduces vertebral fracture risk and invasive ER-positive breast cancer risk, but has no proven reduction in hip fracture risk
Reduces hip fracture risk only, with no effect on vertebral fractures
Reduces non-vertebral fracture risk only, but increases the risk of invasive breast cancer
items.e: In the MORE trial, raloxifene (a selective oestrogen receptor modulator) significantly reduced the risk of vertebral fractures and decreased the risk of invasive ER-positive breast cancer, but did not reduce hip or non-vertebral fracture risk.
items.note: Factually precise question on SERM pharmacology and trial findings.

items.q: According to the ASBMR Task Force recommendations, a 65-year-old woman who has completed 5 years of continuous oral alendronate therapy is evaluated for a drug holiday. Which of the following patient profiles supports initiating a 2- to 3-year bisphosphonate drug holiday?
o: Incident vertebral fracture during the initial 5 years of therapy
History of a fragility hip fracture prior to starting therapy
Femoral neck T-score of -2.1 with no prior history of fragility fracture
items.e: A bisphosphonate drug holiday (2-3 years) is appropriate after 5 years of oral bisphosphonate therapy in patients who are not at high risk (femoral neck T-score above -2.5 and no prior hip or vertebral fragility fractures). High-risk patients should continue therapy up to 10 years or switch agents.
items.note: Accurate guideline-based question on bisphosphonate drug holiday criteria.

items.q: A 52-year-old male presents with acute severe pain and swelling of the first metatarsophalangeal joint. Synovial fluid analysis under compensated polarized light microscopy demonstrates needle-shaped monosodium urate crystals. When aligned parallel to the axis of the red compensator, what key features do these crystals exhibit?
o: Blue color with strongly positive birefringence
Yellow color with strongly negative birefringence
Yellow color with weakly positive birefringence
Blue color with weakly negative birefringence
items.e: Monosodium urate (MSU) crystals in gout are needle-shaped and exhibit strongly negative birefringence. They display a yellow color when aligned parallel to the compensator axis (and blue when perpendicular).
items.note: Accurate, classic exam question with unambiguous standard findings.

items.q: A 54-year-old patient presents with acute pseudogout of the knee joint. Radiographs reveal chondrocalcinosis. Because the patient is under 60 years of age, a workup for the four main metabolic associations ('4 H's' of CPPD) is indicated. Which set of baseline laboratory investigations is most appropriate to screen for these associations?
o: Serum copper, ceruloplasmin, TSH, and anti-TPO antibodies
Ferritin and transferrin saturation, serum calcium, magnesium, and alkaline phosphatase
24-hour urinary uric acid, serum creatinine, BUN, and lipid profile
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate, CRP, rheumatoid factor, and anti-CCP antibodies
items.e: The '4 H's' associated with CPPD are Haemochromatosis (ferritin and transferrin saturation), Hyperparathyroidism (calcium), Hypomagnesaemia (magnesium), and Hypophosphatasia (low alkaline phosphatase).
items.note: Directly tests high-yield clinical screening criteria for CPPD metabolic associations.

items.q: Radiographs of the foot in a patient with long-standing foot pain reveal 'punched-out' juxta-articular erosions with sclerotic margins and overhanging edges (Martel sign). The joint space is preserved and there is no periarticular osteopenia. These radiographic findings are classic for:
items.e: Chronic tophaceous gout classically demonstrates punched-out juxta-articular erosions with sclerotic margins and overhanging edges (Martel sign). Joint space is preserved until late, and periarticular osteopenia is characteristically absent (unlike rheumatoid arthritis).
items.note: Clear diagnostic radiologic distinction between gout and rheumatoid arthritis.

items.q: Prior to initiating allopurinol for hyperuricaemia in patients of Han Chinese, Thai, Korean, or African-American descent, screening for which genetic allele is recommended to prevent severe allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome (SJS/TEN)?
items.e: Allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome (including SJS/TEN and DRESS) is strongly associated with the HLA-B5801 allele. Screening is recommended in high-risk ethnic groups (Han Chinese, Korean, Thai, and African-American) before starting allopurinol.
items.note: Important guideline-backed pharmacological screening recommendation.

items.q: A 45-year-old female presents with acute, excruciating shoulder pain. Radiographs show an ill-defined, translucent, fluffy calcification in the supraspinatus tendon. According to Uhthoff's classification of calcific tendinitis, in which phase is the patient experiencing maximum pain due to macrophage influx and vascular invasion?
items.e: The resorptive phase of Uhthoff's classification is the most painful. In this phase, cell-mediated resorption with macrophage and vascular invasion turns the deposit into a soft, toothpaste-like material, often appearing translucent and ill-defined on radiographs.
items.note: Tests key clinicopathological correlation of Uhthoff's stages.

items.q: According to the ACR 2020 guidelines and the AGREE trial protocol for managing an acute gout flare, what is the recommended low-dose oral colchicine dosing schedule?
o: 1.2 mg immediately, followed by 0.6 mg one hour later
0.6 mg every 2 hours until symptoms resolve or diarrhoea ensues
1.2 mg IV as a single slow bolus
0.5 mg once daily starting 5 days after flare onset
items.e: The AGREE trial established that low-dose colchicine (1.2 mg stat followed by 0.6 mg 1 hour later) is as effective as high-dose regimens for an acute gout flare, with significantly lower rates of side effects such as diarrhoea. IV colchicine is not used.
items.note: Standard guideline-level pharmacology question.

items.q: Synovial fluid from an elderly woman with rapid glenohumeral joint destruction and a massive rotator cuff tear (Milwaukee shoulder) reveals non-birefringent basic calcium phosphate (BCP/hydroxyapatite) crystal aggregates. Which of the following stains is specifically used to visualize these crystals under light microscopy?
items.e: Basic calcium phosphate (hydroxyapatite) crystals are non-birefringent under polarized light microscopy and appear as tiny clumps ('shiny coins'). They are selectively stained using Alizarin red S.
items.note: High-yield pathology stain facts specific to BCP disease.

items.q: An 82-year-old woman presents with acute onset of severe neck pain, fever, neck stiffness, and markedly elevated inflammatory markers. Computed tomography (CT) reveals dense radiopaque calcification surrounding the dens of the axis within the transverse ligament of the atlas. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.e: Crowned dens syndrome is a manifestation of CPPD in the spine, characterized by acute neck pain, fever, and stiffness in elderly patients due to CPP crystal deposition around the dens (transverse ligament), visible on CT.
items.note: Distinctive spinal CPPD presentation commonly tested in entrance exams.

items.q: A 72-year-old man with long-standing Paget disease of the left femur presents following a fall with acute, severe hip pain. Radiographs reveal a displaced intracapsular femoral neck fracture through pagetic bone. Which of the following is the most appropriate definitive management for this fracture?
o: Closed reduction and fixation with multiple cannulated cancellous screws
Open reduction and dynamic hip screw fixation
Hip arthroplasty (hemiarthroplasty or total hip arthroplasty)
Valgus subtrochanteric osteotomy and blade plate fixation
items.e: Femoral neck fractures in pagetic bone carry a very high rate of delayed union and non-union when treated with internal fixation. Therefore, arthroplasty (hemiarthroplasty or total hip arthroplasty) is the preferred treatment.
items.note: Accurate, clear, exam-relevant concept directly supported by standard textbooks and notes.

items.q: A 42-year-old man presents with deep foot pain due to recurrent metatarsal stress fractures and a lateral subtrochanteric femoral pseudofracture. Biochemical work-up reveals normal serum calcium, normal serum phosphate, normal PTH, and a characteristically low total serum alkaline phosphatase (ALP). Which of the following is the most appropriate management principle?
o: Intravenous zoledronic acid single 5 mg infusion
Oral alendronate 40 mg daily for 6 months
Enzyme replacement therapy with asfotase alfa while strictly avoiding bisphosphonates
Oral calcitriol combined with calcium carbonate supplementation
items.e: A low serum ALP is the laboratory hallmark of hypophosphatasia (ALPL gene mutation). Bisphosphonates are strictly contraindicated because they are inorganic pyrophosphate analogues that further inhibit bone mineralisation; treatment includes enzyme replacement with asfotase alfa.
items.note: High-yield topic for SS exam; stem and options are precise and correct.

items.q: A 52-year-old woman is evaluated for chronic musculoskeletal aches and fatigue. Plain radiographs of the hand demonstrate subperiosteal cortical resorption specifically along the radial aspect of the middle phalanges of the index and middle fingers. Which biochemical profile is expected in this patient?
o: Low serum calcium, high serum phosphate, elevated PTH
High serum calcium, low serum phosphate, elevated PTH
Normal serum calcium, normal serum phosphate, markedly elevated ALP
Low serum calcium, high serum phosphate, low PTH
items.e: Subperiosteal resorption on the radial side of the middle phalanges of the index and middle fingers is pathognomonic of primary hyperparathyroidism, which typically displays elevated serum calcium, suppressed or low phosphate, and an inappropriately elevated PTH level.
items.note: Classic pathognomonic radiographic sign paired with standard biochemical findings.

items.q: Which gene encoding sequestosome-1 (p62), a key regulatory protein in the RANK/NF-kB signalling pathway of osteoclasts, is mutated in approximately 40% of familial cases of Paget disease of bone?
items.e: Mutations in SQSTM1 (sequestosome-1, encoding p62) account for about 40% of familial and 5-10% of sporadic cases of Paget disease of bone.
items.note: Direct genetic fact testing a frequently asked molecular target in Paget disease.

items.q: An 18-month-old infant with restricted nutritional intake presents with leg pain, irritability, and pseudoparalysis. Radiographs reveal a dense White line of Frankel and a radiolucent Trummerfeld zone in the metaphysis. Which specific skeletal region is primarily affected by defective osteoid formation in this condition?
items.e: Scurvy (vitamin C deficiency) causes defective collagen hydroxylation and osteoid production by osteoblasts, specifically impairing the metaphysis (primary spongiosa) of long bones.
items.note: Clear, accurate anatomical/pathological distinction for scurvy.

items.q: A 48-year-old farmer from an endemic district in India presents with severe axial spinal rigidity and progressive lower limb weakness. Radiographs show diffuse osteosclerosis of the spine and pelvis with extensive ossification of the interosseous membranes of the forearm and leg. What is the fundamental microstructural change responsible for bone dense brittleness in this condition?
o: Accumulation of glucocerebroside inside marrow macrophages
Substitution of hydroxyl ions by fluoride in hydroxyapatite forming fluorapatite
Failure of 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity leading to unmineralised osteoid accumulation
Excessive osteoclastic resorption yielding a mosaic jigsaw cement line pattern
items.e: In skeletal fluorosis, fluoride replaces hydroxyl groups in hydroxyapatite crystals to form fluorapatite. This increases skeletal density but results in mechanically weak, brittle bone with dense ligamentous and interosseous membrane calcification.
items.note: Relevant to the Indian context, factually sound, correct options.

items.q: In patients with end-stage renal disease undergoing long-term haemodialysis, which of the following is currently recognized as the most common histological type of renal osteodystrophy identified on bone biopsy?
o: Pure osteomalacia secondary to aluminium overload
items.e: Adynamic bone disease (characterized by low bone turnover and low PTH) has become the most common pattern of renal osteodystrophy in modern dialysis populations.
items.note: Standard fact modernizing classic renal osteodystrophy teaching.

items.q: A 68-year-old man with known extensive polyostotic Paget disease presents with a 2-month history of intense, new-onset pain in his left pelvis accompanied by a rapidly enlarging local soft-tissue mass. Radiographs confirm cortical destruction. Which histopathological entity accounts for the majority of secondary malignant transformations in Paget disease?
items.e: Pagetic sarcomatous transformation occurs in under 1% of patients and carries a very poor prognosis. Osteosarcoma is the most common histological subtype arising in pagetic bone.
items.note: Classic, well-established question with clean options and accurate rationale.

items.q: According to the ARCO 2019 criteria for risk factor association in osteonecrosis of the femoral head (ONFH), which threshold of corticosteroid administration defines glucocorticoid-associated ONFH?
o: More than 500 mg prednisolone equivalent over 6 months, diagnosed within 1 year
More than 1 g prednisolone equivalent over 1 month, diagnosed within 6 months
More than 2 g prednisolone equivalent within a 3-month period, diagnosed within 2 years
More than 5 g prednisolone equivalent within a 1-year period, diagnosed within 3 years
items.e: Under ARCO 2019 criteria, glucocorticoid-associated ONFH is defined as receiving over 2 g prednisolone (or equivalent) within a 3-month period, with ONFH diagnosed within 2 years of use (excluding other risk factors).
items.note: Accurate, well-worded, high-yield question directly testing ARCO 2019 diagnostic parameters.

items.q: During a surgical dislocation approach (Ganz) to the hip, preserving the main arterial supply to the femoral head relies on understanding the course of the deep branch of the medial femoral circumflex artery (MFCA). How does this artery run relative to the surrounding musculature?
o: Anterior to obturator externus and posterior to short external rotators
Posterior to obturator externus and anterior to the short external rotators
Posterior to quadratus femoris and anterior to adductor magnus
Anterior to pectineus and posterior to adductor longus
items.e: The deep branch of the MFCA passes posterior to the obturator externus and anterior to the short external rotators (gemelli and obturator internus). This precise anatomical course allows preservation of the femoral head blood supply during surgical dislocation of the hip.
items.note: Anatomically precise, core concept in hip preservation surgery tested in SS exams.
items.reason: repeats fai20261120_063 (MFCA course in Ganz approach)

items.q: A surgeon is performing core decompression for Ficat Stage II non-traumatic osteonecrosis of the femoral head. Which surgical step is essential to avoid the primary non-articular complication of this procedure?
o: Placing the guide wire entry site at or above the level of the lesser trochanter
Advancing the drill bit past the subchondral plate directly into articular cartilage
Creating the drill track entering strictly below the lesser trochanter
Using an 8 mm trephine combined with thermal capsular cauterisation
items.e: Positioning the entry hole below the lesser trochanter creates a stress riser in the subtrochanteric region, leading to subtrochanteric fracture (the main complication). The guide wire entry site must be placed at or above the level of the lesser trochanter to prevent this.
items.note: High-yield surgical pearl with clear distractors and a single correct option.

items.q: A 62-year-old female presents with sudden-onset severe pain over the medial aspect of her right knee, worse at night. Which feature distinguishes spontaneous osteonecrosis of the knee (SONK / SIFK) from secondary osteonecrosis of the knee?
o: Presence of multiple bilateral lesions involving both epiphysis and metaphysis
Presentation in a patient under 45 years of age taking long-term steroids
Single epiphyseal lesion on the medial femoral condyle in an older female
Definitive final outcome requiring urgent bilateral total knee arthroplasty
items.e: SONK (spontaneous osteonecrosis of the knee) typically occurs in women over 55-60 years as a single epiphyseal lesion on the weight-bearing medial femoral condyle, often secondary to subchondral insufficiency fracture. In contrast, secondary osteonecrosis occurs in younger patients (<45 years), is associated with risk factors like steroids, and features multiple/bilateral lesions extending to the metaphysis.
items.note: Classic exam comparison between SONK and secondary AVN of the knee.

items.q: On magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the hip, which finding on T2-weighted sequences is considered pathognomonic for osteonecrosis of the femoral head?
o: Diffuse bone marrow oedema extending continuously into the intertrochanteric crest
Subchondral low-signal line that is convex to the articular cartilage surface
"Double-line sign" consisting of an inner high-signal line beside an outer low-signal line
Single low-signal serpiginous band seen exclusively on T1-weighted images
items.e: The T2-weighted "double-line sign" is pathognomonic of osteonecrosis. It consists of an inner high-signal line representing hyperaemic granulation tissue next to an outer low-signal line representing sclerotic bone at the reactive interface.
items.note: Factually sound, unambiguous imaging question.

items.q: An AP radiograph of the ankle taken 7 weeks after open reduction and internal fixation of a talar neck fracture demonstrates a subchondral radiolucent band across the talar dome (Hawkins sign). What does this finding indicate?
o: Complete avascular necrosis with impending structural collapse
Intact vascularity of the talar body and a low risk of osteonecrosis
Imminent non-union of the fracture site requiring bone graft
Active bacterial osteomyelitis of the talar body
items.e: A positive Hawkins sign (subchondral radiolucency of the talar dome at 6-8 weeks) indicates intact blood supply. Bone resorption causing the subchondral lucency can only occur if disuse osteopenia is mediated by an intact vascular supply, indicating low risk of AVN.
items.note: Standard trauma/metabolic exam concept regarding talar neck fractures.

items.q: According to the Japanese Investigation Committee (JIC) classification system for osteonecrosis of the femoral head, which category carries the highest risk of subchondral collapse?
o: Type A (necrotic lesion confined to the medial third)
Type B (necrotic lesion involving the medial two-thirds)
Type C1 (necrotic lesion extending beyond two-thirds but within the acetabular edge)
Type C2 (necrotic lesion extending lateral to the acetabular edge)
items.e: The JIC classification assesses the location of necrosis relative to the weight-bearing area. Type C2 lesions, which extend lateral to the acetabular edge, carry the highest risk of femoral head collapse, whereas Type A (medial third) lesions rarely collapse.
items.note: Precise classification question testing anatomical risk stratification of ONFH.

items.q: A 30-year-old female in her third trimester of pregnancy presents with left hip pain. MRI shows diffuse marrow oedema extending across the femoral head, neck, and intertrochanteric region, without a focal subchondral band or double-line sign. What is the most appropriate management strategy?
o: Immediate core decompression with stem cell augmentation
Protected weight bearing and analgesia, as the condition is self-limiting
Urgent total hip arthroplasty to prevent acetabular destruction
Vascularised fibular grafting to restore subchondral bone integrity
items.e: The clinical picture and diffuse MRI oedema (without a focal low-signal band or double-line sign) describe transient osteoporosis of the hip, common in third-trimester pregnancy. It is self-limiting over 6 to 12 months and is managed non-operatively with protected weight bearing to prevent fracture.
items.note: High-yield differential diagnosis and management question contrasting TOH with AVN.

items.q: A 5-year-old child presents with short stature, osteosclerosis, recurrent fractures, delayed closure of cranial sutures, and acro-osteolysis of the distal phalanges. Histological examination shows normal osteoclast numbers but an inability of osteoclasts to degrade the organic collagen matrix. A mutation in which of the following enzymes is responsible for this condition (pyknodysostosis)?
items.e: Pyknodysostosis is caused by a deficiency of cathepsin K, a lysosomal cysteine protease secreted by osteoclasts at the ruffled border to digest type I collagen. Carbonic anhydrase II and TCIRG1 mutations cause osteopetrosis due to defective acidification of the resorption compartment.
items.note: The clinical triad of osteosclerosis, delayed suture closure, and acro-osteolysis is pathognomonic for pyknodysostosis, and the enzyme defect is correctly identified.

items.q: Which of the following skeletal dysplasias or metabolic disorders is characterized by histopathological abnormalities predominantly localized to the reserve (resting) zone of the physeal growth plate?
items.e: The reserve (resting) zone of the physis is affected in Gaucher disease, diastrophic dysplasia, pseudoachondroplasia, and Kniest dysplasia. Achondroplasia involves the proliferative zone, while rickets and Schmid metaphyseal chondrodysplasia affect the hypertrophic zone.
items.note: The classification of physeal disorders by zone is a high-yield exam topic and the options are correctly categorized.

items.q: A 32-year-old man sustains a displaced closed diaphyseal fracture of the femur treated with reamed intramedullary nailing. Which statement correctly describes the changes in cortical blood flow following reaming of the medullary canal?
o: Flow remains centrifugal because periosteal vessels are obliterated
Flow becomes centripetal as the periosteal blood supply becomes dominant
Flow in the inner two-thirds of the cortex increases immediately to compensate for periosteal loss
Flow ceases entirely across all cortical layers for at least 6 months
items.e: Normal flow in mature long bones is centrifugal (inside-out, driven by the high-pressure endosteal/nutrient system supplying the inner two-thirds of the cortex). Reaming or displaced fractures disrupt the endosteal supply, causing blood flow to temporarily reverse and become centripetal (outside-in), driven by low-pressure periosteal vessels.
items.note: The physiological response of bone blood flow to trauma and reaming is a standard concept in orthopaedic basic science.

items.q: Which of the following statements regarding osteocalcin is correct?
o: It is the most abundant non-collagenous protein in bone matrix and its synthesis is vitamin K-dependent
It is produced by osteoclasts during the reversal phase of bone remodelling
It is an un-carboxylated structural fibril that provides tensile strength to osteoid
It is a urinary marker of bone resorption unaffected by 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D levels
items.e: Osteocalcin (bone Gla protein) is synthesized by osteoblasts and is the most abundant non-collagenous protein in bone. Its gamma-carboxylation depends on vitamin K, its production is stimulated by 1,25(OH)2D, and serum osteocalcin serves as a marker of bone formation.
items.note: The question accurately tests the biochemical properties and clinical significance of osteocalcin as per the reference notes.

items.q: According to the bioelectric properties of bone under mechanical loading, which of the following correctly describes the piezoelectric charge generated across bone surfaces?
o: The compression side becomes electropositive, leading to bone resorption
The compression side becomes electronegative, stimulating bone formation
The tension side becomes electronegative, stimulating bone resorption
The tension side becomes electronegative, stimulating bone formation
items.e: Bone exhibits piezoelectric properties where mechanical stress produces electric charges: the compression side develops a negative charge (electronegative), which promotes bone formation, whereas the tension side becomes positive (electropositive), promoting bone resorption.
items.note: The relationship between mechanical strain, electrical charge, and cellular response (Wolff's law mechanism) is correctly stated.

items.q: Sclerostin is a key negative regulator of bone formation targeted by the therapeutic monoclonal antibody romosozumab. Which cell type is the primary source of sclerostin secretion, and which pathway does it inhibit?
o: Mesenchymal stem cells; Indian hedgehog pathway
items.e: Sclerostin is secreted predominantly by mature osteocytes embedded in lacunae. It binds to LRP5/6 co-receptors to inhibit the canonical Wnt/beta-catenin signalling pathway, thereby decreasing osteoblastogenesis and bone formation.
items.note: The cell of origin and the molecular target of sclerostin are accurately represented.

items.q: In distraction osteogenesis (Ilizarov technique) following a low-energy corticotomy, bone formation at the distraction gap occurs primarily by which mechanism and at what standard rate?
o: Endochondral ossification at 0.5 mm per day
Intramembranous ossification at 1.0 mm per day
Appositional cartilage formation at 2.0 mm per day
Endochondral ossification at 1.0 mm per day
items.e: Distraction osteogenesis generates new bone via intramembranous ossification (direct bone formation without a cartilage intermediate). The standard distraction protocol is 1.0 mm per day (typically 0.25 mm four times daily) following a latency period of 5 to 7 days.
items.note: The mechanism and rate are standard Ilizarov principles found in Campbell's and the provided notes.

items.q: Nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates such as zoledronate and alendronate exert their potent anti-resorptive effect by inhibiting which key enzyme within osteoclasts?
items.e: Nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates inhibit farnesyl pyrophosphate (FPP) synthase in the mevalonate pathway. This prevents prenylation of essential small GTP-binding proteins (Ras, Rho, Rab), leading to loss of the ruffled border, cell dysfunction, and osteoclast apoptosis.
items.note: The biochemical target of nitrogenous bisphosphonates is a frequent and specific exam question.

items.q: A 72-year-old male is undergoing a total knee replacement for osteoarthritis. Analysis of the non-osteoarthritic, age-matched portion of his articular cartilage would most likely show which of the following changes compared to a 20-year-old?
items.e: With normal aging, keratan sulfate increases while chondroitin-4 sulfate, water content, and chondrocyte number decrease. This results in a decreased chondroitin:keratan sulfate ratio.
items.note: The question correctly tests the distinction between aging and osteoarthritis based on GAG composition and water content as per standard orthopaedic texts.

items.q: Which zone of the articular cartilage contains the highest concentration of proteoglycans and the lowest water content?
items.e: The deep (radial) zone has the highest proteoglycan content and the lowest water content. The superficial zone has the highest water and collagen content but the lowest proteoglycan content.
items.note: This is a fundamental fact regarding the zonal anatomy of articular cartilage frequently tested in postgraduate exams.

items.q: A 62-year-old female with early-stage knee osteoarthritis is noted to have 'softening' of the cartilage on arthroscopy. Pathophysiologically, this early chondromalacia is primarily driven by which matrix change?
o: Decreased water content and decreased permeability
Increased water content and increased permeability
items.e: In early osteoarthritis, damage to the collagen network allows the matrix to swell, leading to increased water content and increased permeability, which decreases the stiffness of the cartilage.
items.note: The question accurately reflects the early pathological sequence of OA where water content increases, unlike in normal aging.

items.q: Which cell type in the synovial intima is responsible for the production of hyaluronic acid and lubricin?
items.e: Type B synoviocytes are fibroblast-like cells of mesenchymal origin that produce the key components of synovial fluid, including hyaluronic acid and lubricin. Type A cells are macrophage-like and phagocytic.
items.note: The distinction between Type A and Type B synoviocytes is a classic basic science topic in orthopaedics.

items.q: A 25-year-old athlete sustains a full-thickness chondral injury of the femoral condyle that penetrates the subchondral bone. What is the characteristic feature of the repair tissue that will fill this defect?
o: Hyaline cartilage with Type II collagen
Fibrocartilage with predominantly Type I collagen
Calcified cartilage with Type X collagen
items.e: Full-thickness (osteochondral) injuries breach the subchondral bone, allowing marrow mesenchymal stem cells to form a fibrin clot that matures into fibrocartilage, which is dominated by Type I collagen and is mechanically inferior to hyaline cartilage.
items.note: The question correctly identifies the difference between partial-thickness (no healing) and full-thickness (fibrocartilage repair) injuries.

items.q: During dynamic joint motion, which mode of lubrication is generally regarded as the primary mechanism for reducing friction between articular surfaces?
items.e: Elastohydrodynamic lubrication, where cartilage deforms to increase contact area and trap a fluid film, is the main mode during dynamic motion. Boundary lubrication (lubricin) is important at low speeds and high loads.
items.note: Lubrication mechanisms are high-yield topics; the question correctly identifies the primary mode during motion.

items.q: A 70-year-old male presents with acute knee pain and swelling. Synovial fluid analysis reveals rhomboid-shaped crystals that are weakly positively birefringent under polarized light. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.e: Calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate (CPPD) crystals, seen in pseudogout, are rhomboid or rod-shaped and show weak positive birefringence (appearing blue when parallel to the compensator axis).
items.note: Crystal identification is a standard part of synovial fluid analysis in orthopaedic exams.

items.q: Based on the results of the SUMMIT trial (Saris et al., 2014), which statement is true regarding the treatment of symptomatic knee cartilage defects of 3 cm² or larger?
o: Microfracture is superior to MACI at 2 years
MACI is superior to microfracture at 2 years
Both techniques have identical outcomes for large defects
Debridement alone is the treatment of choice
items.e: The SUMMIT trial demonstrated that Matrix-induced Autologous Chondrocyte Implantation (MACI) was superior to microfracture for symptomatic knee defects ≥ 3 cm² in terms of pain and function at 2 years.
items.note: The SUMMIT trial is the primary evidence base for choosing MACI over microfracture for larger defects in modern orthopaedics.

items.q: A 70-year-old male with severe right hip osteoarthritis is advised to use a walking cane. According to the biomechanics of the hip in single-leg stance, how does using a cane in the contralateral (left) hand primarily reduce the joint reaction force (JRF) on the right hip?
o: By increasing the force produced by the ipsilateral abductor muscles
By providing a long lever arm that produces a moment to counter body weight
By shifting the body’s center of gravity lateral to the hip joint
By reducing the effective weight of the lower limb during the swing phase
items.e: Using a cane in the contralateral hand provides a long lever arm from the hip, which creates a moment that assists the abductor muscles in countering body weight. This significantly reduces the required abductor muscle force and, consequently, the total joint reaction force by 40-60%.
items.note: The question correctly identifies the biomechanical principle of lever arms and moments in hip joint loading as per standard texts.

items.q: An orthopaedic resident is comparing the material properties of various implants. Which of the following correctly ranks the materials in descending order of their Young’s modulus of elasticity (E)?
o: Cobalt-chrome > Stainless steel > Titanium alloy > Cortical bone
Alumina ceramic > Titanium alloy > Stainless steel > PMMA
Stainless steel > Cobalt-chrome > Cortical bone > Titanium alloy
Alumina ceramic > Cobalt-chrome > Cortical bone > Titanium alloy
items.e: The correct order of stiffness (modulus) from highest to lowest is: Ceramic (alumina) > Cobalt-chrome (~210-230 GPa) > Stainless steel (~190-200 GPa) > Titanium alloy (~110 GPa) > Cortical bone (~15-20 GPa) > PMMA > Polyethylene.
items.note: The ranking is accurate and follows the standard values provided in the reference notes.

items.q: A surgeon is performing a bridge plating for a comminuted midshaft femoral fracture. Based on Perren’s strain theory, what is the required interfragmentary strain level to promote the formation of secondary bone healing (callus)?
items.e: According to Perren's strain theory, interfragmentary strain under 2% leads to primary bone healing (absolute stability), while strain between 2% and 10% promotes secondary bone healing with callus (relative stability). Strain over 10% leads to non-union.
items.note: The strain thresholds are standard AO principles and match the reference notes.

items.q: To increase the stability of a uniplanar external fixator construct in a distal tibial fracture, which of the following modifications provides the most significant increase in construct stiffness?
o: Adding a second parallel connecting rod (stacking)
Decreasing the distance between the connecting rod and the bone
Increasing the diameter of the Schanz pins
Increasing the distance between the two pins within a single fragment
items.e: The stiffness of an external fixator pin is proportional to the fourth power of its radius (r^4). Therefore, increasing the pin diameter is the most effective way to increase the overall stiffness of the construct.
items.note: The r^4 relationship makes pin diameter the most influential factor in fixator stiffness.

items.q: In the manufacturing of highly cross-linked polyethylene (HXLPE) for total hip arthroplasty, the polymer is often 'remelted' after irradiation. What is the primary mechanical consequence of this remelting process?
o: It increases the yield strength and toughness of the material
It eliminates free radicals but reduces the fatigue strength
It stabilizes free radicals while increasing the Young's modulus
It increases the resistance to delamination and pitting in TKA
items.e: Remelting (heating above the melting point) effectively eliminates free radicals, preventing long-term oxidation, but it results in a decrease in the material's fatigue strength, toughness, and yield strength compared to annealing.
items.note: The trade-off between oxidation resistance and mechanical strength in HXLPE processing is a classic exam topic.

items.q: A 45-year-old patient undergoes a longitudinal cortical window (open-section defect) for the excision of a benign bone tumor. Compared to a small circular drill hole of the same width, how does this open-section defect affect the torsional strength of the bone?
o: It reduces torsional strength by approximately 10-20%
It has no significant difference compared to a round hole
It reduces torsional strength drastically, potentially by up to 90%
It increases the area moment of inertia, thereby strengthening the bone
items.e: An open-section defect, such as a longitudinal slot or window, acts as a severe stress riser and reduces the torsional strength of the bone drastically (often quoted up to 90%), much more than a round or oval hole.
items.note: The distinction between the weakening effects of holes versus slots is a standard biomechanical fact.

items.q: During the preparation of polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) bone cement, which chemical agent is included in the liquid monomer component to act as a stabilizer/inhibitor, preventing premature polymerisation during storage?
items.e: The liquid component of bone cement contains the MMA monomer, DMPT (the accelerator), and hydroquinone. Hydroquinone is added to prevent the monomer from polymerizing spontaneously during storage.
items.note: The chemical constituents of PMMA and their specific roles are frequently tested.

items.q: Titanium alloy (Ti-6Al-4V) is widely used in uncemented femoral stems due to its biocompatibility and lower modulus. However, which of the following is a specific disadvantage of titanium that limits its use in certain implant components?
o: It is more prone to crevice corrosion than 316L stainless steel
It has poor wear resistance and is unsuitable as a bearing surface
It has a higher modulus of elasticity than cobalt-chromium
It does not allow for osseointegration or porous coating
items.e: Titanium has poor wear resistance (it is relatively soft) and produces debris if used as a bearing surface. It is also notch sensitive, meaning surface scratches can lead to fatigue failure. It is, however, excellent for osseointegration and has a lower modulus than steel or CoCr.
items.note: The material limitations of titanium, specifically regarding wear and notch sensitivity, are well-documented.

items.q: A 28-year-old male sustains a high-velocity gunshot wound to the thigh. During exploration of the sciatic nerve, the surgeon notes a 'neuroma-in-continuity' where the nerve is visibly enlarged but the epineurium is intact. Despite waiting for 4 months, there has been no clinical recovery and the Tinel sign has not advanced. This injury corresponds to which Sunderland grade?
items.e: Sunderland Grade IV is a neuroma-in-continuity where the axons, endoneurium, and perineurium are disrupted, but the epineurium remains intact. Unlike grades II and III, it does not show an advancing Tinel sign and requires surgical excision and repair.
items.note: The question accurately reflects the Sunderland classification and the clinical behavior of a Grade IV injury as described in the reference notes.

items.q: A surgeon is performing a nerve repair and inadvertently creates a small longitudinal incision in the perineurium. Which of the following is the most likely immediate clinical consequence of this specific injury?
o: Interruption of the mesoneurial blood supply
Wallerian degeneration of the entire nerve
items.e: The perineurium provides the main tensile strength of the nerve and maintains intrafascicular pressure; a cut in this layer leads to fascicular herniation. It also serves as the blood-nerve barrier.
items.note: This is a classic exam fact regarding the function of the perineurium and the consequence of its injury.

items.q: A 45-year-old patient presents with an anaesthetic arm following a motorcycle accident. Electrodiagnostic studies performed 4 weeks later demonstrate an absent motor response (CMAP) in the median nerve, but the sensory nerve action potential (SNAP) is found to be preserved. What does this finding imply?
o: The nerve is in a state of neurapraxia
The dorsal root ganglion has been destroyed
items.e: In preganglionic injuries (root avulsions), the dorsal root ganglion (DRG) remains intact and connected to the distal sensory axon. Therefore, the SNAP remains preserved even though the limb is anaesthetic. Postganglionic injuries result in loss of both SNAP and CMAP.
items.note: This is a high-yield 'key exam fact' for orthopaedic superspeciality exams regarding brachial plexus injuries.

items.q: In the physiological classification of nerve fibres, which of the following fibres is the first to be blocked by local anaesthetics?
items.e: Local anaesthetics block small, myelinated fibres first. The typical order is B (preganglionic autonomic) > A-delta and C (pain, temperature) > A-beta (touch) > A-alpha (motor). Pressure/tourniquets block large fibres first.
items.note: The question correctly tests the sequence of local anaesthetic blockade based on fibre type and size.

items.q: According to the sliding filament theory of muscle contraction, which component of the sarcomere maintains a constant length as the muscle shortens?
items.e: The A band represents the full length of the myosin (thick) filaments and remains constant during contraction. The I band and H zone shorten as actin slides over myosin, bringing the Z lines closer together.
items.note: This is a fundamental concept in muscle physiology frequently tested in basic science sections.

items.q: A 30-year-old athlete experiences sudden, sharp pain in the back of the thigh during the 'braking' phase of a sprint. An MRI confirms a grade II hamstring strain at the myotendinous junction. Which type of muscle contraction is most likely responsible for this injury?
items.e: Eccentric contractions (muscle lengthening while contracting) generate the greatest force and are the most common cause of muscle strains, typically occurring at the myotendinous junction of two-joint muscles like the hamstrings.
items.note: The clinical scenario perfectly matches the physiological principles of eccentric muscle injury.

items.q: During an elective orthopaedic procedure under general anaesthesia, the anaesthesiologist notes a rapid rise in end-tidal CO2 and tachycardia, followed by muscle rigidity. Which of the following is the most likely molecular basis for this condition?
o: Antibodies to the postsynaptic nicotinic ACh receptor
items.e: Malignant hyperthermia is most commonly caused by an autosomal dominant mutation in the RYR1 gene, leading to uncontrolled calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum when triggered by volatile anaesthetics or succinylcholine.
items.note: The question tests the molecular pathology and clinical presentation of a critical anaesthetic complication relevant to orthopaedic surgery.

items.q: Which of the following sensory receptors is classified as 'slowly adapting' and is specifically tested using Semmes-Weinstein monofilaments for early detection of compression neuropathy?
items.e: Merkel discs are slowly adapting receptors responsible for static touch and pressure. Semmes-Weinstein monofilaments are a threshold test for these fibres and are the most sensitive test in early compression neuropathy. Meissner and Pacinian corpuscles are rapidly adapting.
items.note: The question correctly identifies the receptor type and the clinical utility of the Semmes-Weinstein test.

items.q: A research team plans to investigate the risk factors associated with a very rare complication of total hip arthroplasty that occurs in fewer than 1 in 10,000 cases. Which study design is most appropriate and efficient for this objective?
items.e: Case-control studies start with the outcome and look back for exposures, making them the most efficient and practical design for studying rare diseases or outcomes with long latency periods.
items.note: Correctly identifies the primary strength of the case-control design as per the provided notes.

items.q: In a clinical trial comparing two different surgical techniques for ACL reconstruction, which of the following methods is uniquely capable of balancing both known and unknown confounding variables between the treatment groups?
items.e: Randomization is the only method in clinical research that can balance both known and unknown confounders between groups, ensuring that any observed difference is likely due to the intervention.
items.note: Matches the 'Exam pearl' and experimental design section of the reference notes.

items.q: A study utilizes a large hospital database to identify all patients who underwent intramedullary nailing for tibial fractures over the last 10 years. It compares the union rates between smokers and non-smokers based on existing medical records. What is the level of evidence for this study according to the JBJS therapeutic hierarchy?
items.e: Retrospective comparative studies, such as this retrospective cohort study based on medical records, are classified as Level III evidence.
items.note: Correctly applies the levels of evidence hierarchy for therapeutic studies provided in the notes.

items.q: A new diagnostic test for periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) is tested in two different patient populations: one in a specialized tertiary referral center with a high prevalence of infection, and another in a community hospital with a low prevalence. Which of the following parameters will remain constant across both settings?
items.e: Sensitivity, specificity, and likelihood ratios (LR) are intrinsic properties of a test and do not change with disease prevalence. PPV and NPV, however, are highly dependent on the prevalence of the condition in the population being tested.
items.note: Accurately reflects the diagnostic test statistics section of the notes.

items.q: A randomized trial comparing two types of suture material for tendon repair finds no statistically significant difference in the primary outcome (p = 0.15). However, the study was only powered to detect a 20% difference, while the actual difference was 10%. This study is likely suffering from which of the following?
items.e: A Type II error (beta) occurs when a study fails to reject a false null hypothesis (i.e., it misses a real difference). This is most commonly caused by an inadequate sample size (underpowered study).
items.note: Correctly identifies the relationship between power, sample size, and Type II error.

items.q: A researcher wants to compare the mean post-operative flexion (a continuous, normally distributed variable) between two independent groups of patients: those who received a 'fast-track' rehabilitation protocol and those who received 'standard' care. Which statistical test is most appropriate?
items.e: The unpaired (Student's) t-test is the standard parametric test used to compare the means of two independent groups when the data is continuous and follows a normal distribution.
items.note: Correctly applies the statistical test selection table from the notes.

items.q: When interpreting Patient-Reported Outcome Measures (PROMs) in orthopaedic research, which of the following scores is designed such that a higher numerical value indicates a worse clinical outcome or greater disability?
items.e: The DASH and QuickDASH (Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand) are scored from 0 to 100, where higher scores indicate greater disability. The Oxford, Constant, and Harris Hip scores all use higher values to represent better function.
items.note: Correctly identifies the directionality of common orthopaedic PROMs as listed in the notes.

items.q: A surgeon develops a radiation-induced cataract after years of performing fluoroscopy-guided trauma procedures. According to the ICRP (2011) thresholds, what is the absorbed dose threshold for this deterministic effect?
items.e: Cataracts are deterministic effects (tissue reactions) with a threshold; in 2011, the ICRP lowered the threshold for the lens of the eye to 0.5 Gy. Skin erythema has a higher threshold of approximately 2 Gy.
items.note: The question accurately reflects the updated ICRP threshold mentioned in the reference notes.

items.q: Which interaction between X-ray photons and tissue is primarily responsible for the occupational radiation dose received by the surgical team in the operating room?
items.e: Compton scatter occurs when a photon interacts with an outer-shell electron and changes direction; it is the dominant interaction at higher energies in soft tissue and the main source of occupational dose to staff. The photoelectric effect involves complete absorption and is responsible for image contrast and patient dose.
items.note: The question correctly identifies Compton scatter as the primary source of staff dose as per the notes.

items.q: To minimize occupational radiation exposure during fluoroscopic procedures, which of the following is the most appropriate positioning strategy for the surgical team?
o: Stand on the X-ray tube side during lateral views
Stand on the image intensifier side during lateral views
Invert the C-arm so the X-ray tube is on top of the patient
Keep the image intensifier as far from the patient as possible
items.e: Scatter radiation is greatest on the X-ray tube (entrance) side of the patient. To minimize dose, the surgeon should stand on the image intensifier side and keep the intensifier as close to the patient as possible.
items.note: The original question combined AP and lateral concepts awkwardly. The fix focuses on the most critical safety principle for staff positioning.

items.q: A CT scan is performed for a complex tibial plateau fracture in a patient with a previous stainless steel intramedullary nail. Which of the following would help REDUCE the 'beam hardening' and 'photon starvation' artifacts?
o: Increasing the kVp and using a metal artifact reduction (MAR) algorithm
items.e: Metal artifacts like beam hardening (streaks) can be reduced by using higher kVp and mAs, thinner reconstructions, metal artifact reduction (MAR) algorithms, and dual-energy CT. Titanium implants produce significantly less artifact than stainless steel or cobalt-chrome.
items.note: The question correctly identifies the technical parameters required to mitigate metal artifacts on CT.

items.q: A 42-year-old premenopausal woman with a history of a fragility fracture is sent for a DEXA scan. Which score should be used to interpret her bone mineral density (BMD) relative to age-matched controls?
items.e: Z-scores compare the patient's BMD to the mean of age- and sex-matched individuals and are used for premenopausal women, men under 50, and children. T-scores compare BMD to young healthy adults and are reserved for postmenopausal women and men aged 50 or over.
items.note: The question correctly distinguishes between T-score and Z-score applications based on patient demographics.

items.q: An MRI of the spine is ordered to evaluate for early discitis. Which sequence is most sensitive for detecting marrow oedema but is also robust when used near metallic spinal hardware?
items.e: STIR (Short Tau Inversion Recovery) is an inversion recovery sequence that nulls fat signal and is the most sensitive for marrow oedema (bone bruises, infection, occult fractures). It is also more robust near metal than chemical fat-saturated sequences.
items.note: The question correctly identifies STIR as the sequence of choice for marrow oedema near metal.

items.q: On an MRI of the ankle, the peroneal tendons appear to have increased signal intensity on T1-weighted images as they curve around the lateral malleolus, but appear normal on T2-weighted images. This phenomenon is likely due to:
items.e: The magic angle effect occurs when collagen fibres are oriented at approximately 55 degrees to the static magnetic field (B0). This causes increased signal on short-TE sequences (T1, PD, GRE) which mimics pathology but disappears on long-TE sequences (T2).
items.note: The question accurately describes the classic presentation and diagnostic feature of the magic angle artifact.

items.q: Which of the following conditions is most likely to appear as a 'cold' (photopenic) lesion on a Technetium-99m MDP bone scan?
items.e: Multiple myeloma, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, and purely lytic metastases (such as from renal or thyroid cancer) often appear as cold lesions because they do not trigger a sufficient osteoblastic response. Osteoid osteoma and Paget's disease typically show intense 'hot' uptake.
items.note: The question correctly identifies multiple myeloma as a classic cause of a photopenic lesion on bone scan.

items.q: A 68-year-old male is scheduled for an urgent hemiarthroplasty for a hip fracture. His medical history is significant for a myocardial infarction 2 months ago and severe aortic stenosis. According to the ASA physical status classification, what is his preoperative grade?
items.e: ASA IV is defined as a severe systemic disease that is a constant threat to life; examples include a recent myocardial infarction (under 3 months) and severe valve disease. Since this is an urgent/emergency surgery for a hip fracture, the suffix 'E' is added.
items.note: The question correctly applies the ASA criteria and the emergency suffix as per the provided reference notes.

items.q: During a prolonged spinal fusion surgery for scoliosis, at what point should the anaesthetist redose the prophylactic cefazolin, assuming no massive haemorrhage has occurred?
o: Only if the case exceeds 12 hours
items.e: Standard guidelines recommend redosing cefazolin every 4 hours during surgery to maintain adequate tissue levels. Redosing is also indicated if blood loss exceeds 1500 mL.
items.note: The redosing interval for cefazolin is a standard fact supported by the reference notes.

items.q: A patient is scheduled for a total hip arthroplasty under spinal anaesthesia. He has been receiving prophylactic enoxaparin (LMWH) 40 mg once daily for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis due to prior immobilisation. According to ASRA guidelines, what is the minimum required interval between the last dose of LMWH and the spinal needle insertion?
items.e: For patients on prophylactic-dose LMWH, the American Society of Regional Anesthesia (ASRA) recommends a minimum interval of 12 hours before performing a neuraxial block. For therapeutic-dose LMWH, the interval is 24 hours.
items.note: The timing for neuraxial anesthesia in the context of LMWH is correctly stated according to ASRA guidelines in the notes.

items.q: A 70-year-old female with rheumatoid arthritis is scheduled for a total knee arthroplasty. She currently takes methotrexate 15 mg weekly and adalimumab (a TNF-alpha inhibitor) every 2 weeks. According to the 2022 ACR/AAHKS guidelines, how should these be managed perioperatively?
o: Withhold methotrexate for 2 weeks; continue adalimumab
Continue methotrexate; withhold adalimumab and schedule surgery in the third week after the last dose
Withhold both methotrexate and adalimumab for 4 weeks prior to surgery
Continue both medications to prevent a rheumatoid flare
items.e: Current guidelines recommend continuing conventional DMARDs like methotrexate throughout the perioperative period. Biologics like adalimumab should be withheld; surgery should be scheduled at the end of the dosing cycle (e.g., for a 2-week cycle, operate in week 3).
items.note: The management of DMARDs and biologics matches the 2022 ACR/AAHKS guidelines cited in the notes.

items.q: Which regional anaesthetic technique is preferred for postoperative analgesia in total knee arthroplasty because it provides effective pain relief while better preserving quadriceps strength for early mobilisation?
items.e: The adductor canal block is a sensory-dominant block that preserves quadriceps motor strength better than a femoral nerve block, thereby reducing the risk of falls and facilitating early mobilisation after TKA.
items.note: The clinical advantage of the adductor canal block over the femoral nerve block is a standard orthopaedic teaching point found in the notes.

items.q: A 52-year-old male with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes and a 30-pack-year smoking history presents with an infected tibial nonunion. There is a through-and-through cortical defect, and the construct is mechanically unstable. According to the Cierny-Mader classification, how should this patient's clinical stage be documented?
items.e: Anatomical Type IV refers to diffuse, mechanically unstable lesions (e.g., infected nonunion). The host is Bs (systemic compromise) due to diabetes and smoking. Type III is localized and stable; Bl refers to local compromise like lymphedema.
items.note: The question accurately applies the Cierny-Mader staging system for both anatomical type (unstable nonunion = IV) and physiological host (systemic factors = Bs) as per the reference notes.

items.q: According to the consensus definition of fracture-related infection (FRI) published by Metsemakers et al. and updated in 2020, which of the following is considered a confirmatory criterion, as opposed to a suggestive criterion?
o: New or persistent wound drainage beyond the first few days
Presence of a sinus tract communicating with the bone or implant
Raised serum inflammatory markers (ESR and CRP)
A single deep tissue culture positive for Staphylococcus aureus
items.e: Confirmatory criteria for FRI include a fistula/sinus communicating with bone/implant, purulent drainage, phenotypically indistinguishable pathogens in ≥2 deep samples, or specific histopathology. Wound drainage, raised markers, and single cultures are only suggestive criteria.
