items.note: The question correctly distinguishes between confirmatory and suggestive criteria for FRI based on the 2018/2020 consensus definitions cited in the notes.

items.q: A 45-year-old gardener presents with a well-defined lucent lesion in the distal tibial metaphysis. MRI shows a characteristic rim of slightly higher T1 signal lining the abscess cavity. This finding, which helps distinguish subacute osteomyelitis from a bone tumor, is known as the:
items.e: The penumbra sign on T1-weighted MRI represents a rim of vascularized granulation tissue lining an abscess cavity and is highly characteristic of subacute osteomyelitis (Brodie's abscess). The paprika sign refers to healthy bleeding bone during debridement.
items.note: The penumbra sign is a classic radiological pearl for Brodie's abscess mentioned in the reference notes and standard texts.

items.q: In the management of a 6-cm segmental femoral defect following radical debridement for chronic osteomyelitis, a surgeon utilizes the Masquelet induced-membrane technique. What is the recommended timing for the second stage (spacer removal and bone grafting)?
items.e: The second stage of the Masquelet technique is typically performed at 4-8 weeks. This allows for the formation of a vascular membrane that secretes growth factors like VEGF, TGF-beta, and BMP-2 before it becomes too fibrotic or loses its inductive capacity.
items.note: The timing for the Masquelet technique is a standard board-exam fact and is correctly stated in the reference notes.

items.q: A 55-year-old patient with a 35-year history of chronic osteomyelitis of the femur presents with a new fungating mass and foul-smelling discharge at the site of a long-standing sinus tract. Biopsy confirms squamous cell carcinoma. What is the most likely diagnosis and the standard treatment?
items.e: A Marjolin ulcer is a squamous cell carcinoma arising in a long-standing chronic osteomyelitis sinus tract (latency is usually decades). The standard treatment for this aggressive malignancy in the context of chronic infection is typically amputation.
items.note: The clinical presentation and treatment of Marjolin ulcer are accurately described and supported by the reference notes.

items.q: A 28-year-old sexually active female presents with migratory polyarthralgia and tenosynovitis of the wrist. On examination, she has several painless pustules on her extremities. Synovial fluid aspiration from a mildly swollen knee reveals a WBC count of 40,000 cells/mm3. What is the most likely organism and the appropriate initial antibiotic?
items.e: The triad of tenosynovitis, dermatitis (pustules), and migratory polyarthralgia is classic for disseminated gonococcal infection. N. gonorrhoeae is the most common cause of septic arthritis in healthy young adults. Treatment is IV ceftriaxone 1g daily.
items.note: The clinical triad for gonococcal arthritis is a classic exam topic. The WBC count of 40,000 is also typical for gonococcal cases, which often present with lower counts than other pyogenic infections.

items.q: A 28‑year‑old woman presents with chronic low back pain and a swollen right knee that has been painful for the past 4 months. Baseline ESR is 65 mm h⁻¹ and Mantoux induration is 15 mm. Synovial fluid analysis shows 18 000 WBC/mm³, predominantly lymphocytes, high protein and low glucose. Which investigation is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
o: Synovial fluid culture on Lowenstein–Jensen medium
MRI of the knee with contrast
items.e: GeneXpert MTB/RIF on a biopsy or tissue sample provides rapid detection of M. tuberculosis and rifampicin resistance. Synovial cultures are slow and often negative in paucibacillary disease, while MRI is useful for extent but not diagnosis.
items.note: All facts come directly from the notes and standard guidelines.

items.q: Which of the following is the earliest radiographic sign of tuberculous spondylitis?
o: Disc space narrowing with paradiscal osteopenia
items.e: Disc space narrowing with paradiscal osteopenia (early fat‑loss of marrow) appears before vertebral collapse or gibbus formation. Ivory vertebrae are seen in other conditions like lymphoma.
items.note: Note explicitly states this as the earliest sign.
items.reason: repeats main bank b711 (earliest sign of spinal TB)

items.q: A 7‑year‑old child with nocturnal hip pain wakes up crying and denies fever. Plain radiograph shows a preserved joint space but an irregularly eroded femoral head. Which joint involvement pattern is most characteristic of tuberculous arthritis in children?
o: Early joint space loss with rapid erosions
Marginal erosions in the periphery with a preserved articular cartilage
Diffuse synovial hypertrophy causing early ankylosis
items.e: Tuberculous arthritis starts with marginal erosions of the bare areas; cartilage is spared until late, so joint space remains preserved initially.
items.note: Matches pediatric TB arthritis description.

items.q: A 45‑year‑old woman with chronic knee pain has a synovial biopsy showing caseating granulomas. GeneXpert MTB/RIF is negative. Which test should be performed next to rule out drug‑resistant disease?
o: Line probe assay for INH and RIF resistance
MRI of the knee with contrast
items.e: After a negative GeneXpert, a line probe assay on the tissue specimen provides rapid detection of isoniazid and rifampicin resistance, the surrogate for multidrug‑resistant TB.
items.note: Consistent with national diagnostic algorithm.

items.q: A 2‑year‑old child presents with bowed legs, a widened wrist, and delayed closure of the anterior fontanelle. Serum 25(OH)D is 10 ng/mL, calcium is 8.5 mg/dL, phosphate 2.0 mg/dL, and PTH is 80 pg/mL. Which disorder best explains this biochemical profile?
items.e: The low 25(OH)D with high PTH, low phosphate and normal calcium is classic for nutritional vitamin D deficiency rickets.
items.note: All facts match standard references.

items.q: A 14‑year‑old boy with progressive bowing of the legs, hearing loss and dental enamel hypoplasia has a serum phosphate of 2.5 mg/dL, calcium of 9.0 mg/dL, PTH of 45 pg/mL, and a normal 1,25(OH)₂D level. Which laboratory finding is most likely to be elevated?
items.e: Low phosphate with normal calcium and inappropriately normal 1,25(OH)₂D points to FGF23‑mediated phosphaturia, typical of X‑linked hypophosphataemic rickets.
items.note: Consistent with the biochemical profile of XLH.

items.q: The first-line investigation to confirm anuric phosphate loss in a child suspected of phosphopenic rickets is:
items.e: Low tubular maximum for phosphate (TmP/GFR) calculated from a 24‑hour urine confirms phosphaturia.
items.note: Standard diagnostic approach.

items.q: Which of the following is a typical clinical feature of hypophosphatasia that differentiates it from other forms of rickets/osteomalacia?
items.e: Hypophosphatasia has a low ALP due to ALPL mutation; other forms have raised ALP.
items.note: Directly taken from notes.

items.q: A 68‑year‑old woman with a DXA T‑score of –2.8 at the femoral neck and a single wrist fracture 3 months ago is being started on osteoporosis therapy. Which of the following drugs is most appropriate to begin treatment?
items.e: The patient has a recent fragility fracture and a T‑score < –2.5, qualifying her for antiresorptive therapy. Alendronate is the first‑line, inexpensive oral agent for such a profile.
items.note: Clear first‑line oral bisphosphonate use.

items.q: A 72‑year‑old man on alendronate for 6 years, with a creatinine clearance of 38 mL/min, now reports mild dysphagia. Which of the following statements is true regarding his medication?
o: He should discontinue alendronate immediately due to renal dysfunction
Oral bisphosphonates are contraindicated when CrCl < 35 mL/min, but 38 mL/min is acceptable
Switching to IV zoledronate would require an even higher renal clearance
He should add calcium and vitamin D to mitigate dysphagia
items.e: Alendronate is contraindicated when CrCl < 35 mL/min. A CrCl of 38 mL/min is borderline but still considered acceptable; monitoring is advised.
items.note: Direct match to renal threshold.

items.q: Which of the following is NOT a typical adverse effect of IV zoledronate administered as a 5‑mg infusion?
o: Acute phase reaction with fever and myalgia
Hypocalcaemia in patients with inadequate vitamin D
items.e: Oesophageal ulcers are associated with oral bisphosphonates; IV zoledronate does not cause oesophageal irritation.
items.note: Clear differentiation of route‑specific side‑effects.

items.q: A 58‑year‑old man presents with a sudden, excruciating pain in the first metatarsophalangeal joint, erythema, and warmth. Joint aspiration shows needle‑shaped, strongly negatively birefringent crystals that appear yellow when parallel to the compensator axis. Which of the following serum values is most likely to be abnormal?
items.e: The picture is classic for acute gout. Elevated serum urate (>6.8 mg/dL) is the metabolic abnormality that precipitates monosodium urate crystal deposition.
items.note: Correct

items.q: During the diagnostic work‑up of a patient with crystal arthritis, which specimen must always be sent for Gram stain and culture to rule out septic arthritis?
items.e: The presence of crystals does not exclude infection; therefore joint fluid should always be cultured and Gram‑stained when crystal arthritis is suspected.
items.note: Correct

items.q: An elderly patient has chronic joint pain and radiographs show a ‘punched‑out’ erosion with sclerotic margins and overhanging edges. Which crystal disease is most likely responsible?
items.e: These radiographic changes—Martel sign or ‘rat‑bite’ erosion—are characteristic of chronic tophaceous gout.
items.note: Correct
items.reason: repeats main bank b332 (punched-out erosions of gout)

items.q: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of monosodium urate crystals under compensated polarised light microscopy?
o: Yellow when parallel to compensator axis
items.e: Monosodium urate crystals are needle‑shaped, strongly negatively birefringent, and appear yellow when parallel to the compensator. Positive birefringence is incorrect.
items.note: Correct

items.q: A patient with a history of chronic tophaceous gout develops a sudden, painful swelling of the right elbow. Synovial fluid analysis reveals >70,000 WBC per mm³. Which of the following should be considered immediately?
o: Reassure, as it is an acute gout flare
items.e: WBC >70,000 may mimic sepsis; septic arthritis must be ruled out first, hence high‑dose antibiotics and culture are indicated.
items.note: Correct

items.q: In patients with calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease, what is the most specific imaging modality to detect crystal deposits when aspiration is not possible?
items.e: Ultrasound with the double‑contour sign is the most specific bedside modality for CPPD when aspirate is unavailable; DECT is excellent for urate but less specific for CPPD.
items.note: Correcting answer

items.q: A 52‑year‑old man with longstanding hyperuricaemia is started on allopurinol 300 mg daily. On day 3, he develops a flare of arthritis. Which of the following statements best describes the management strategy?
o: Discontinue allopurinol until the flare resolves
Start a low‑dose colchicine to cover the flare
Wait for the flare to self‑resolve before starting allopurinol
items.e: Allopurinol can be continued during an acute flare; a short course of low‑dose colchicine provides symptomatic relief while urate‑lowering continues.
items.note: Correct

items.q: Which laboratory finding would help differentiate Paget disease from a solitary osteoblastic metastasis when both show a high total alkaline phosphatase?
items.e: Normal serum calcium is typical of Paget disease, whereas osteoblastic metastases may cause hypercalcaemia; urinary hydroxyproline is a resorption marker that rises in metastatic disease.
items.note: Standard biochemical differentiation cited in orthopaedic texts.

items.q: In a patient with extensive polyostotic Paget disease, which of the following complications is least likely?
o: Osteolytic lytic lesions with normal ALP
items.e: Osteolytic lesions with normal ALP are not typical; Paget disease is characterized by mixed lytic and sclerotic lesions with raised ALP. Other options are recognised complications.
items.note: Matches the complications overview.
items.reason: flawed premise (lytic phase of Paget is recognised) and overlaps b1164

items.q: A 70‑year‑old man with known Paget disease of the pelvis is scheduled for total hip replacement. Which intra‑operative complication is most likely because of the underlying bone pathology?
o: Intra‑operative fracture of the femoral neck
items.e: Pagetic bone is enlarged but mechanically weaker; during THA the femoral neck or subtrochanteric region is prone to intra‑operative fractures.
items.note: Based on the described mechanical weakness in the notes.

items.q: An MRI of a patient with suspected early osteonecrosis of the femoral head shows a serpiginous low‑signal band on T1 and a double‑line appearance on T2. What does the inner high‑signal line represent?
o: Granulation tissue forming the reactive interface.
Residual necrotic bone with fatty marrow.
Synovial fluid tracking into the subchondral region.
items.e: The inner hyperaemic granulation tissue (high‑signal on T2) borders the outer low‑signal sclerotic bone, giving the classic double‑line sign of osteonecrosis.
items.note: Matches standard MRI description.

items.q: Which imaging modality is **best** for screening the contralateral hip in a patient newly diagnosed with unilateral osteonecrosis of the femoral head?
o: CT scan of the femoral head
items.e: MRI is about 99 % sensitive and can detect early, pre‑radiographic disease in the asymptomatic hip.
items.note: Standard of care from notes.
items.reason: repeats cai20261111_026 (MRI most sensitive for early ONFH)

items.q: In osteonecrosis of the femoral head, subchondral collapse typically begins when:
o: Cell death of osteocytes occurs within the first 48 h.
The necrotic bone undergoes constant remodeling without resorption.
The interface between dead and living bone is resorbed during repair.
The marrow fat hypertrophies and extravascular pressure rises immediately after injury.
items.e: Collapse occurs during repair; resorption at the dead‑living junction weakens the subchondral plate, leading to a crescent sign and flattening.
items.note: Consistent with pathophysiology described.
items.reason: repeats cai20261120_w14_093 (timing of collapse in ONFH)

items.q: Which of the following **is not** a common non‑traumatic cause of osteonecrosis of the femoral head?
o: Alcohol consumption >400 ml pure ethanol per week
items.e: Radiation is a recognised but uncommon cause; the most frequent non‑traumatic etiologies are steroids, alcohol, and haemoglobinopathies such as sickle cell disease.
items.note: No controversy.

items.q: A 42‑year‑old male with newly diagnosed osteonecrosis of the femoral head is found on radiograph to have a crescent sign on frog‑leg lateral view. What does this finding indicate?
o: Early stage with no risk of progression.
Established subchondral fracture and imminent collapse.
Full femoral head collapse has already occurred.
Normal variation in bone density for adults.
items.e: The crescent sign— a subchondral radiolucent line—marks a subchondral fracture and predicts impending collapse.
items.note: Classic imaging sign.

items.q: The size and location of the necrotic lesion on MRI are considered the most important prognostic factors for which outcome in osteonecrosis of the femoral head?
items.e: Lesion size (especially >30 % of the femoral head) and location (medial/central) predict poor prognosis and the need for THA.
items.note: Directly from notes.

items.q: A 28‑year‑old woman presents with dull ache in the forearm after a heavy load. MRI shows low‑signal cortical thickening without fracture line. Which of the following is the earliest radiologic change of a bone stress injury?
o: Periosteal oedema followed by marrow oedema
items.e: Periosteal oedema appears first (grade 1), then marrow oedema (grade 2), a visible fracture line (grade 4) and finally callus (grade 3).
items.note: All facts align with accepted grading of stress fractures.
items.reason: repeats main bank b1117 (earliest MRI sign of stress injury)

items.q: A 45‑year‑old man with chronic rheumatoid arthritis develops patchy periarticular osteoporosis on plain radiographs. Which cell type is primarily responsible for this change?
items.e: Osteoclasts resorb bone, producing the characteristic patchy loss of mineral observed in CRPS type 1 and rheumatoid arthritis.
items.note: Standard bone biology understanding.

items.q: The mineralising front in articular cartilage is marked by a line that separates which two cartilage zones?
items.e: The tidemark delineates the boundary between uncalcified and calcified cartilage.
items.note: Anatomical cartilage knowledge.

items.q: A 62‑year‑old man is undergoing evaluation for osteoporosis. Which serum marker is most specific for ongoing bone formation?
o: C‑terminal telopeptide of type I collagen (CTX)
N‑terminal propeptide of type I collagen (P1NP)
items.e: P1NP is released during the synthesis of type I collagen and is widely used as a bone‑formation marker.
items.note: Marker specificity per bone metabolism guidelines.

items.q: A 50‑year‑old man presents with medial knee pain and a radiograph shows a 4‑mm full‑thickness defect in the femoral condyle. Which histological feature of articular cartilage would most likely be altered in this patient’s lesion?
o: Increase in type I collagen fibres
Loss of type VI collagen around chondrocytes
Presence of calcified cartilage within the defect
items.e: In osteoarthritic cartilage the earliest reversible change is loss of proteoglycans, primarily aggrecan. The other options describe changes not typical of early OA or of fissure defects.
items.note: Valid, single‑best answer.

items.q: During a routine arthroscopic evaluation of a 30‑year‑old athlete, the synovium appears pale, smooth, and thin. Which molecule is most likely deficient in the synovial fluid?
items.e: Normal synovium produces lubricin, a boundary lubricant that maintains a frictionless surface. A paucity of lubricin leads to a pale, rough synovium often seen in early OA.
items.note: Clear, single‑best answer.

items.q: A 65‑year‑old woman has knee pain and MRI shows a thickened articular cartilage layer. Histology reveals an increased proportion of type I collagen in the superficial zone. This finding is best explained by:
o: Increased anabolism of type I collagen by chondrocytes
Replacement of type II by type I collagen in hypertrophic chondrocytes
Aging‑related shift from type II to type I collagen in cartilage
Chronic inflammatory cytokine stimulation causing fibrocartilage formation
items.e: With age, the proportion of type I collagen rises relative to type II, especially in the superficial zone, reflecting a transition toward a less resilient matrix.
items.note: Correct, single‑best answer.
items.reason: invented premise (age-related type II to type I collagen shift)

items.q: Which of the following statements best describes the role of pericellular type VI collagen in articular cartilage?
o: Forms the bulk of the matrix giving compressive strength
Anchors collagen fibrils to the subchondral bone
Surrounds chondrocytes and regulates their function
Cross‑links aggrecan aggregates to resist shear stress
items.e: Type VI collagen is a pericellular matrix protein that surrounds individual chondrocytes, influencing cell–matrix interactions and signaling. It is not a bulk structural component.
items.note: Valid, single‑best answer.

items.q: A 22‑year‑old patient with a traumatic meniscal tear has a partial coronal defect in the meniscus. Arthroscopic microfracture is performed. Which type of cartilage is most likely to populate the defect?
items.e: Microfracture recruits marrow‑derived cells that typically form fibrocartilage, which is mechanically inferior to the native hyaline cartilage of the joint surface.
items.note: Correct, single‑best answer.

items.q: The Donnan osmotic pressure in articular cartilage is primarily generated by:
o: Fixed negative charges of proteoglycan GAGs attracting cations
Positive charge of type II collagen fibers
Calcium crystals in the calcified zone
Synovial fluid pH changes during loading
items.e: Proteoglycan GAGs carry negative charges that create an osmotic swelling pressure, counterbalanced by the collagen network and responsible for compressive stiffness.
items.note: Accurate, single‑best answer.

items.q: In a 15‑year‑old girl suspected of growth plate injury, X‑ray shows a cleft extending from the femoral shaft to the articular surface. Which collagen type is predominantly present in the hypertrophic zone of this physeal cartilage?
items.e: The hypertrophic zone of the growth plate contains type X collagen, associated with mineralisation and eventual endochondral ossification.
items.note: Correct, single‑best answer.

items.q: During MRI of a patient with early osteoarthritis, the T2 relaxation time is markedly prolonged in the deep zone of cartilage. This change most likely reflects:
o: Loss of proteoglycan content leading to increased water mobility
Excessive synovial fluid accumulation in the joint cavity
items.e: Loss of proteoglycans reduces fixed charge density, allowing more free water and increased T2 relaxation. This is an early, reversible OA change.
items.note: Correct, single‑best answer.

items.q: A 62‑year‑old man with a stable distal femur fracture is being planned for intramedullary nailing. The surgeon decides to use a titanium alloy nail. What is the most likely consequence of this choice in terms of stress shielding?
o: Greater stress shielding than a steel nail
Less stress shielding than a steel nail
Stress shielding only occurs with cobalt‑chrome implants
items.e: Titanium alloy (E≈110 GPa) is closest to cortical bone (E≈15‑20 GPa) and therefore produces the least stress shielding compared with a higher‑modulus steel nail.
items.note: Straightforward application of modulus order.

items.q: A 28‑year‑old female presents with an isolated 5th metatarsal base fracture. Which fracture pattern is most compatible with the tensile‑force mechanism described for this bone?
items.e: The 5th metatarsal base is commonly fractured by a transverse, avulsion pattern due to tensile loading at its base.
items.note: Standard biomechanical fracture pattern.

items.q: In a free‑body diagram of a lever system, which of the following statements about the moment produced by a force is correct?
o: Moment is independent of the lever arm length
Moment equals force divided by the lever arm
Moment is force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the axis
Moment only exists in third‑class levers
items.e: Moment (torque) = force × perpendicular distance from the fulcrum, the fundamental definition used in all lever classes.
items.note: Basic definition of torque.

items.q: A patient receives a cemented total hip arthroplasty using PMMA bone cement. Which property of PMMA makes it suitable for this application?
o: Highest modulus of elasticity among all implant materials
Low toughness leading to rapid failure
Lower modulus than cortical bone to reduce stress shielding
High brittleness allowing precise shaping during surgery
items.e: PMMA’s modulus (~2‑3 GPa) is intermediate and closer to cortical bone than metal, helping to reduce stress shielding compared with a metal stem.
items.note: Standard biomechanical rationale for bone cement.

items.q: On a stress–strain curve of a metallic alloy, the region where the slope is linear and deformation is fully recoverable is known as the:
items.e: The elastic region is linear, with stress directly proportional to strain; deformation is reversible upon unloading.
items.note: Fundamental material property.

items.q: Which material property best describes the ability of an implant to absorb energy before breaking?
items.e: Toughness is defined as the area under the stress–strain curve, indicating how much energy an implant can absorb before failure.
items.note: Standard definition.

items.q: A 28‑year‑old gymnast develops flashing pain and an inability to dorsiflex the right ankle after a fall. Electromyography shows a conduction block over the common peroneal nerve at the fibular head, but axon remains intact. Which of the following best explains the early loss of motor function with preservation of sensation?
o: Injury to the dorsal root ganglion
Compression of the entire nerve segment
Selective loss of large‑diameter fibers due to ischemia
items.e: A neurapraxic injury causes focal demyelination of the large motor A‑alpha fibers, producing a conduction block; sensory A‑beta fibers are less affected, so sensation remains intact.

items.q: A new surgical technique for shoulder arthroplasty is compared with the standard procedure in a poster‑randomised trial. The investigators stratify randomisation by surgeon experience and use concealed centralized allocation. Which statement best describes the role of this design feature?

It balances measured and unmeasured confounders across groups
It allows calculation of a relative risk instead of an odds ratio
It guarantees 100% follow‑up for all enrolled patients

items.note: Graded design element matches answer B.

items.q: A systematic review includes five RCTs evaluating a pharmaceutical for osteoarthritis. Two trials have high risk of bias, the others are low risk. The reviewers downgrade the evidence on the basis of inconsistency. Which GRADE criterion is being applied?

items.note: Direct correspondence to GRADE.

items.q: A registry follows a cohort of patients after shoulder arthroplasty for 10 years. It reports a 5% revision rate. Which of the following is a limitation of using a registry for evaluating implant survivorship?

Revision is a crude endpoint with limited clinical detail
It is susceptible to recall bias

items.q: An investigator performs a retrospective cohort study using hospital records to compare early mobilization vs delayed mobilization after knee replacement. The loss to follow‑up is 25%. According to the bias table, this situation most likely introduces which type of bias?

items.q: A 55‑year‑old patient undergoes a lumbar spine CT scan. Which of the following best explains why the patient receives a higher effective dose compared to a single AP chest radiograph?

Larger field of view increases total photon exposure
CT uses continuous exposure with a rotating tube, accumulating dose over time
The patient’s body habitus is larger, requiring higher mA

Inverse square law is irrelevant in intraoperative fluoroscopy
Rotating the C‑arm allows use of lower mAs

Add 2 mm of aluminium filtration to remove low‑energy photons
Increase mAs from 15 to 30 to sharpen contrast
Reduce source‑to‑image distance from 100 to 80 cm

Minimal photon energy (≈30 keV) and very low mAs in the dual‑energy setup
Extensive beam collimation to a small field of view
Real‑time dose monitoring with incremental adjustments

items.q: A 30‑year‑old intravenous drug user presents with fever, a swollen ankle and a purulent draining sinus around the tibia shaft. Which antibiotic strategy is required to eradicate a biofilm‑forming organism on a loose implant?

items.q: A patient with recurrent discharging sinuses over the distal femur is found to have a skull‑like area of bone destruction and an elevated serum amyloid A level. What long‑term complication is most likely?

items.q: A 28‑year‑old woman from a high‑burden TB area presents with chronic right hip pain, mild swelling, and a soft‑tender mass on the anterolateral thigh. items.q: During antitubercular therapy for a knee joint, which radiographic change represents the first evidence of bone healing?

items.q: A 55‑year‑old woman is prescribed risedronate 35 mg weekly. She is advised to take the tablet with a full glass of water while upright. What is the primary reason for this instruction?

items.e: Oral bisphosphonates have <1 % bioavailability; taking them on an empty stomach with water and staying upright for 30–60 minutes reduces oesophageal irritation and maximises absorption.

items.q: Which of the following is true regarding denosumab in osteoporosis management?

It binds to RANKL, preventing RANK activation

items.note: Accurate, single best answer with correct distractors.

items.q: A 72‑year‑old woman with a history of osteoarthritis complains of new swelling and pain in the left knee. MRI shows cortical destruction and a soft‑tissue mass. Which complication is most likely?
items.e: Paget sarcoma occurs in <1 % of Paget patients, usually presenting as a new lytic lesion with soft‑tissue mass and rapid pain.
items.note: Correct answer is unique and justified; distractors clearly wrong.

items.q: Which of the following sites is least commonly involved in Paget disease?
items.e: The hands and feet are rarely affected; the pelvis, skull and tibia are common sites.

items.q: A 55‑year‑old man with polyostotic Paget disease develops sudden high‑output congestive heart failure. The most likely pathophysiological mechanism is:

items.e: Extensive pagetic bone causes many arteriovenous shunts, increasing cardiac output and leading to high‑output heart failure.
items.note: Accepted pathophysiology.

items.q: In a monostotic Paget lesion of the femur with normal serum calcium and phosphate, an elevated serum alkaline phosphatase is indicative of:
items.e: In monostotic disease the alkaline phosphatase rise reflects the active remodeling phase; calcium/phosphate remain normal unless immobilized.
items.note: Standard biochemical interpretation.

items.q: Which imaging finding is characteristic of the bone-infiltrative phase of Paget disease in the skull?
items.e: The skull in the mixed phase shows a cotton‑wool, lytic pattern with cortical thickening and diploic expansion.
items.note: Classic radiologic description.

items.q: A 42‑year‑old man on chronic oral steroids for rheumatoid arthritis presents with left groin pain that worsens with weight‑bearing. Plain radiograph is normal; MRI shows a serpiginous low‑signal band on T1 and a double‑line sign on T2. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.e: The MRI findings – a serpiginous low‑signal line on T1 and a double‑line sign on T2 – are pathognomonic for osteonecrosis of the femoral head.
items.note: Clear stem‑answer match with Campbell’s description.

items.q: A 36‑year‑old female receives a high‑dose steroid pulse for lupus nephritis. Two months later she develops asymptomatic bilateral femoral head lesions on MRI. According to ARCO 2019 criteria, which of the following best defines steroid‑associated osteonecrosis?
o: Osteonecrosis diagnosed within 1 year of >400 mL ethanol/week
Osteonecrosis within 2 years of >2 g prednisolone in 3 months
Osteonecrosis within 1 month of any steroid use
items.e: ARCO 2019 defines steroid‑associated osteonecrosis as diagnosis within 2 years of receiving >2 g of prednisolone equivalent in a 3‑month period.
items.note: Direct quotation from the reference table.

items.q: Which of the following investigations is the most sensitive for detecting early osteonecrosis before radiographic changes appear?
items.e: MRI is about 99 % sensitive and specific for early (pre‑radiographic) disease, whereas bone scan and CT are less sensitive and plain radiographs are normal early on.
items.note: Consensus from Campbell’s operative orthopaedics.

items.q: A 48‑year‑old patient with sickle cell disease presents with right hip pain. MRI shows the classic double‑line sign with a central area of bone marrow oedema. Which of the following best explains the pathogenesis of osteonecrosis in sickle cell disease?
o: Direct marrow cell toxicity by steroids
Intravascular occlusion by sickled red cells
items.e: In sickle cell disease, sickled erythrocytes occlude the femoral head vasculature, causing ischemia and osteonecrosis.
items.note: Pathophysiology matches the reference.

items.q: On plain radiograph of a hip with osteonecrosis, a subchondral radiolucent line is seen on frog‑leg lateral view. This is known as the:
items.e: The subchondral radiolucent line on a frog‑leg lateral is the crescent sign, indicating a subchondral fracture.
items.note: Eponym matches standard teaching.

items.q: Which of the following is a common risk factor for idiopathic osteonecrosis in Indian patients?
items.e: Recent reports from India show post‑COVID‑19 steroid use as a frequent cause of idiopathic osteonecrosis.

items.e: The deep branch of the medial femoral circumflex artery runs posterior to obturator externus; the Ganz approach preserves it, maintaining femoral head perfusion.
items.note: Anatomical detail from the notes.

items.q: A 28‑year‑old man presents with a forearm fracture after a trivial fall. Radiographs show a narrow, slightly lucent line with a surrounding thin radiolucent halo and no mass effect. Which feature of bone composition most likely explains the initial radiographic appearance of this type of fracture?
o: The high proportion of cellulose in bone
The presence of osteoid gaps between collagen fibrils where mineral first nucleates
The predominance of type II collagen
The high calcium content of the bone matrix
items.e: The minimal mineralisation in the early, unstressed phase produces a radiolucent halo; this is a consequence of the mineral‑lag that occurs between the collagen scaffold and the deposition of hydroxyapatite.
items.note: Correct mapping of fracture radiology to osteoid mineralisation lag.

items.q: A 4‑year‑old child has a delayed growth plate closure and absence of the clavicular sternal ends. Genetic testing reveals a loss‑of‑function mutation in the RUNX2 gene. Which bone‑matrix protein is directly downstream of RUNX2 and is deficient in this patient?
items.e: RUNX2 activates the transcription of osterix, which is essential for osteoblast differentiation; paucity of osterix explains the skeletal abnormalities seen in cleidocranial dysplasia.
items.note: Direct downstream transcription factor.

items.q: A 60‑year‑old woman on long‑term glucocorticoids has elevated serum CTX but normal serum osteocalcin. Which cellular event is most responsible for the rise in CTX?
o: Increased osteoclast fusion mediated by RANKL
Decreased alkaline phosphatase activity in osteoblasts
items.e: Glucocorticoids up‑regulate RANKL expression on osteoblasts/osteocytes, promoting osteoclastogenesis and bone resorption, thereby elevating CTX.
items.note: Direct link between glucocorticoid‑induced RANKL and resorption marker.

items.q: In a routine bone biochemistry panel, which marker is most specific for ongoing mineralisation (i.e., bone formation) rather than collagen synthesis?
items.e: Bone‑specific alkaline phosphatase hydrolyses pyrophosphate, a mineralisation inhibitor; its activity is confined to the mineralising front of osteoblasts and is therefore the most specific formation marker.

items.note: Direct relation of DMP1 to FGF23.

items.q: Which of the following proteoglycans is the main core protein that carries chondroitin sulfate and keratan sulfate chains in articular cartilage?

items.note: Standard textbook fact

items.q: The boundary line that separates the uncalcified articular cartilage from the calcified zone is called:
items.e: The tidemark is the visible line marking the mineralisation front; the cement line lies just deeper between calcified cartilage and bone.
items.note: Exact anatomical term

items.q: What is the principal role of lubricin (PRG4) in articular cartilage?
items.e: Lubricin is secreted by superficial zone chondrocytes and synoviocytes, functioning as a boundary lubricant to reduce friction during joint movement.
items.note: Clear functional description

items.q: A patient with a full‑thickness cartilage defect undergoes marrow stimulation. Which collagen type predominantly builds the repair tissue?
items.e: Marrow stimulation recruits fibroblasts and progenitor cells that lay down type I collagen, producing fibrocartilage that is mechanically inferior to native hyaline cartilage.
items.note: Standard repair tissue composition

items.q: Which statement best describes the relationship between water content and mechanical properties of intact articular cartilage?

Higher water content increases permeability but reduces strength
Water content is irrelevant to cartilage mechanics
Water content decreases permeability under load

items.note: Direct correlation of biomechanical data

items.e: The superficial zone has the highest chondrocyte density, contributing to shear resistance and lubrication through lubricin secretion.
items.note: Consistent with histological observations

Regenerating axons sprouting in an axonotmetic injury

The perineurium provides the primary tensile strength of the nerve
The perineurium acts as a blood‑nerve barrier but does not influence mechanical strength
Cutting the perineurium leads to immediate axonal regeneration of all fascicles

Neurotmesis of the common peroneal nerve

items.q: During a lumbar spine X‑ray, a 100‑mm magnification is required for a templating study. Which distance adjustment achieves this smallest change in the X‑ray tube to patient distance?

The apron provides no protection to the arms

items.q: A 68‑year‑old woman with a hip fracture is scheduled for primary hemi‑arthroplasty. Her pre‑operative HbA1c is 8.4 %. Which of the following is the best initial step to reduce infection risk before the elective procedure?

items.q: A 65‑year‑old woman on alendronate 70 mg weekly presents with new‑onset dysphagia and odynophagia. Which adverse effect is most likely and how should it be managed?
o: Osteonecrosis of the jaw – stop medication and refer for dental implant
Atypical femoral fracture – obtain a full‑length femur X‑ray
Oesophagitis – advise on proper swallowing technique and give a proton‑pump inhibitor
Acute phase reaction – start an antihistamine pre‑infusion
items.e: Oral bisphosphonates can cause oesophagitis. The patient should be advised to swallow the pill fully, remain upright 30‑60 minutes, and may use a proton‑pump inhibitor if symptoms persist.
items.note: Incorrect options are unrelated to dysphagia.

items.q: Which of the following patients is most appropriate for initiating an anabolic agent such as teriparatide?
o: 58‑year‑old man with T‑score –2.4 and no fractures
70‑year‑old woman with T‑score –2.6 and a recent vertebral fracture
80‑year‑old woman with multiple prior fractures and T‑score –3.2
75‑year‑old man on long‑term steroids with T‑score –2.0
items.e: Anabolic therapy is reserved for very high‑risk patients: recent fracture, T‑score < –3.0, multiple fractures, or high fracture risk scores. Option C meets these criteria.
items.note: Matches guideline indications.

items.q: Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of romosozumab?
o: Antagonises sclerostin, thereby increasing Wnt signalling
Stimulates intermittent PTH‑1‑34 receptors on osteoblasts
items.e: Romosozumab is a monoclonal antibody against sclerostin, lifting its inhibition on Wnt signalling, leading to increased bone formation and decreased resorption.
items.note: Direct drug action fact.

items.q: Which of the following laboratory findings is most characteristic of acute crystal arthritis, irrespective of the crystal type?
o: Joint space narrowing on plain radiograph
items.e: During an acute flare, synovial fluid shows a markedly elevated WBC count (2 000–50 000/mm³, often higher) reflecting intense inflammation. Serum urate levels may be normal, CRP is variable, and radiographs remain normal in the early phase.
items.note: Clear single best answer; distractors are plausible but incorrect.
items.reason: wrong key (crystal arthritis WBC usually below 50,000)

items.q: A 68‑year‑old woman with chronic renal failure presents with knee pain and swelling. Synovial fluid shows weakly positive birefringent, blue‑colored rhomboid crystals. What disease is indicated?
items.e: Weakly positive birefringent, blue crystals are classic for calcium pyrophosphate (CPPD). Gout crystals are strongly negative birefringent and yellow.
items.note: Answer directly matches the crystal description.

items.q: Which of the following imaging techniques is best for detecting monosodium urate deposits when aspiration is impractical?
items.e: DECT colour‑codes the urate deposits, providing a sensitive and specific imaging method for gout when joint aspiration cannot be performed.
items.note: Correct imaging modality is unequivocally DECT.

items.q: A patient with suspected acute pseudogout is found to have a synovial WBC count of 60 000 cells/mm³ and Gram‑negative bacteria on culture. Which statement is true?
o: Crystal arthritis always excludes septic arthritis
Presence of crystals rules out infection
Infection and crystal deposition can coexist; send culture regardless
The WBC count rules out infection
items.e: Crystals and infection can coexist; therefore the fluid must be cultured even when crystals are seen. A high WBC count alone does not exclude septic arthritis.
items.note: Answer reflects standard clinical practice.

items.q: A 62‑year‑old man presents with thigh pain that worsens at night. X‑ray of the femur shows bowing with a transverse ‘banana‑shaped’ fracture. His serum alkaline phosphatase is markedly raised, calcium and phosphate normal. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
items.e: The classic ‘banana’ fracture (transverse subtrochanteric) in a patient with high ALP and normal calcium/phosphate points to Paget disease where the bone is enlarged yet weak.
items.note: Disorder, presentation, labs and imaging all match Paget; distractors are inconsistent.

items.q: Which complication of Paget disease is most likely to respond to alkali phosphonate therapy before surgery is considered?
o: Spinal cord compression from vertebral enlargement
items.e: Bisphosphonates reduce marrow vascularity and bone turnover, often relieving spinal cord compression secondary to epidural “steal” before surgical decompression.
items.note: Therapeutic effect of bisphosphonates.

items.q: A 68‑year‑old patient with progressive femoral bowing develops a painful, incomplete fracture on the convex side. Which statement best describes this fracture?
o: It is an osteoporotic wedge fracture
items.e: In Paget-affected long bones, the convex (tension) side is prone to fissure or stress fractures, which are painful and precede complete breakage.
items.note: Biomechanics of bowed long bone.
